and the Supreme Court Collegium. Recommendations from High Cour t Collegiums 
are yet to be received in respect of 203 vacancies in High Courts. 
 
 During the year 2021, 09 Judges were appointed in the Supreme C ourt, 11 Chief 
Justices, 120 fresh Judges were appointed and 63 Additional Jud ges were made 
permanent across various High Courts. Also in the year 2022, up  to 26.05.2022, 02 
Judges have been appointed in the Supreme Court, 01 Chief Justi ce, 53 Judges were 
appointed in the High Courts and 13 Additional Judges of the Hi gh Courts were made 
permanent across various High Courts. 
 
 Filling up of vacancies in the High Courts is a continuous, int egrated and 
collaborative process between the Executive and the Judiciary. It requires consultation 
and approval from various constitutional authorities both at st ate and central level. 
Hence, the time for filling up of vacancies of the Judges in the higher Judiciary cannot 
b e  i n d i c a t e d .  W h i l e  e v e r y  e f f o r t  i s  m a d e  t o  f i l l  u p  t h e  e x i s t i ng vacancies 
expeditiously, vacancies of Judges in High Courts do keep on ar ising on account of 
retirement, resignation or elevation of Judges and also due to increase in the strength 
of Judges.  
 
3.11 As per the existing Memorandum of Procedure for appointmen t of Judges of High 
Courts, the Chief Justice of the High Court is required to init iate the proposal for filling up of 
vacancies of a Judge in a High Court six months prior to the oc currence of vacancies.  
Government appoints only those persons as Judges of High Courts  who are recommended by 
Supreme Court Collegium (SCC). The primary onus of filling up v acancies in the High Court 
lies with the High Court Collegium. 
 
 As on 26.05.2022, against the sanctioned strength of 1104 Judge s in the High Courts, 
711 Judges are in position, leaving 393 vacancies of Judges to be filled. Against 393 
vacancies, 190 proposals are at various stages of processing be tween the Government 
and the Supreme Court Collegium. Recommendations from High Cour t Collegiums 
are yet to be received in respect of 203 vacancies in High Courts. 
 
 In the year 2021, 251 recommendations were made by the High Cou rt Collegium. So 
far (as on 26.05.2022) out of these 251 recommendations,  
148 appointments have been made in the various High Courts and 74 names were not 
recommended by the Supreme Court Collegium and accordingly remi tted to 
concerned High Courts. This amounts to 30% rejection at the lev el of Supreme Court 
Collegium. Out of the remaining 29 proposals are at various sta ges of processing 
between the Government and the Supreme Court Collegium. 
 
 Filling up of vacancies in the High Courts is a continuous, int egrated and 
collaborative process between the Executive and the Judiciary. It requires consultation 
and approval from various constitutional authorities both at st ate and central level. 

24 
 
Hence, the time for filling up of vacancies of the Judges in the higher Judiciary cannot 
b e  i n d i c a t e d .  W h i l e  e v e r y  e f f o r t  i s  m a d e  t o  f i l l  u p  t h e  e x i s t i ng vacancies 
expeditiously, vacancies of Judges in High Courts do keep on ar ising on account of 
retirement, resignation or elevation of Judges and also due to increase in the strength 
of Judges.  
 
Further observation 
 
3.12 The Committee is not in the agreement with the comments of  the DoJ that "the 
time for filling up of vacancies of the Judges in the higher Ju diciary cannot be 
indicated". The timeline has been drawn in the 2 nd J u d g e s  C a s e  a n d  a l s o  i n  t h e  
Memorandum of Procedure (MOP) regarding appointment of Judges. But regrettably, 
those time lines are not adhere to by both, the Judiciary and t he Executive, which is 
leading to delay in filling up of the vacancies. As per the dat a provided by the 
Government, as on 31.12.2021, there are 3 HCs (Telangana, Patna  and Delhi) where 
vacancies are more than 50% and 10 HCs where vacancies are more  than 40% of their 
respective sanctioned strength. These all are large states, whe re judge to population 
ratio is already skewed and such level of vacancies is a matter  of deep concern. 
Accordingly, the Committee reiterates its recommendations in th i s  r e g a r d .  T h e  
Government and the Judiciary should come up with some out of bo x thinking to deal 
with this perennial problem of vacancies in the HCs.  
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
3.13 Accordingly, the Committee reiterates its recommendation a s referred above and also 
recommends that the entire process of appointment of Judges, particularly at the High Courts, 
should be relooked into. A workable and efficient process, incl uding a proactive timeline 
should be drawn and scrupulously adhered to, by synergizing the  efforts of the Judiciary and 
the Government. (3.10) 
Action Taken 
3.14 
 In order to make the Collegium system of appointments of Judges  of the Supreme 
Court and High Courts more broa d-based, transparent, accountabl e and bringing 
objectivity in the system, the Government brought into force the Constitution (Ninety-
Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointmen ts Commission 
Act, 2014 w.e.f. 13.04.2015. However, both the Acts were challe nged in the Supreme 
Court. The Supreme Court vide Judgment dated 16.10.2015 declare d both the Acts as 
unconstitutional and void. The Collegium system as existing pri or to the enforcement 
of the Constitution (Ninety-Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 was decl ared to be 
operative. Subsequently, the Supreme Court vide order dated 16. 12.2015 directed the 
Government to finalize the exis ting MoP by supplementing it in consultation with the 
Supreme Court Collegium taking into consideration eligibility c riteria, transparency, 
establishment of secretariat and mechanism to deal with complaints.  
 

25 
 
 The Government of India after due deliberations, proposed chang es in the existing 
MoP and the draft MoP’s were sent to the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India vide letter 
dated 22.03.2016. The response of the Chief Justice of India th ereon was received on 
25.05.2016 and 01.07.2016. The views of the Government were con veyed to the 
Chief Justice of India on 03.08.2016. The inputs on the MoP of the Supreme Court 
Collegium was received from Chief Justice of India vide letter dated 13.03.2017. 
 
 In another judgment dated 4.7.2017 of Supreme Court in a “suo m oto” contempt 
proceeding against a Judge of the Calcutta High Court, the Supr eme Court has 
underlined the need to revisit the process of selection and app ointment of Judges to 
the Constitutional Courts. The G overnment of India has conveyed  the need to make 
improvement on the draft MoP to the Secretary General of the Su preme Court vide 
letter dated 11.07.2017. The MoP is under finalization by the G overnment in 
consultation with the Supreme Court Collegium. 
 
Further Observation  
3.15 The Committee is surprised to note that the Supreme Court and the Government 
have failed to reach at a consensus on revision of the Memorand um of Procedure (MOP) 
for appointment of Judges to the constitutional courts, though the same is under 
consideration of both for about seven years now. The Committee expects the 
Government and the Judiciary to finalize the revised MOP, which  is more efficient and 
transparent, in terms of the Supreme Courts observation cited above.  
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.16 Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) were meant to bring down  substantially the 
pendency of cases related to heinous crimes like rape and POCSO  Act at the district and 
subordinate court levels. However after assessing the performan ce of these courts in the past 
two decades the Committee observes that these courts remained ' Fast' in namesake only. 
About 1.84 Lakh cases are presently pending in these FTSCs and as per NCRB data even the 
cases disposed by the FTSCs took anywhere between one to 10 yea rs for their disposal. Lack 
of Judges, rigorous procedures and frequent adjournments are so me of the main reasons for 
dysfunctionality of the fast track courts.  (3.23) 
 
3.17 The Committee, therefore, recommends that in addition to e stablishment of more 
FTSCs the Department should also study and suggest how systemic  improvement may be 
brought about to make the fast track courts truly faster. The C ommittee further recommends 
the Department to explore the best practices in other countries where FTCs are functional and 
have been able to dispose of cases in a time bound manner and t o bring about the required 
changes in our system to make it more efficient. (3.24) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.18 In pursuance of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 2018, the Department of Justice is 
implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Fast Track Special  Courts since October 
2019 for expeditious disposal of rape and POCSO Act cases. 

26 
 
 
3.19 The scheme embarked to establish 1023 Fast Track Special C ourts including 389 
exclusive POCSO Courts in 31 Stat es/UTs for the speedy disposal  and removal of pendency 
of rape and POCSO Act cases. The scheme was initially for a per iod of one year spreading 
over two Financial Years.  
 
3.20 A Third Part Party Evaluation was conducted by the Nationa l Productivity Council in 
2020 which recommended the continuation of the scheme along wit h the following 
recommendations for achieving the overall effectiveness of the FTSCs. These includes:  
 
a. Strengthening of the investigatio n agencies, Forensic Science L aboratories, and 
Victim Compensation Schemes.  
b. Ensuring timely submissions of DNA reports, depute the appropri ate number of 
Public Prosecutors, appropriate number of Vulnerable Witness De position Centres 
(VWCDs) and ensuring child-frien dly response for deposition of testimonies of the 
witnesses.  
c. Regular furnishing of data by t he FTSCs on the online portal of  the Department of 
Justice. 
 
3.21 The recommendations of the NPC were sent to the Law Secret ary of States/UTs, 
Registrar Generals of High Courts and other concerned Ministries for their compliance. 
 
3.22 With respect to best practices followed by other countries ,  i t  h a s  b e e n  f o u n d  t h a t  
Ghana introduced a qualitative standard for speed in the legal system, through the use of 
computers for efficient case management and speedy disposal of c a s e s .  A  t i m e  p e r i o d  
requirement was placed on the disposal of these cases by specif ying that they would have to 
b e  d i s p o s e d  o f  w i t h i n  6  m o n t h s .  A u s t r a l i a  h a s  h a d  a  f a s t  t r a c k  court system in place since 
2006 for deciding commercial and intellectual property disputes. The fast track courts aim for 
the delivery of judgment within 6 weeks of trial through the ab olition of pleadings, 
determination of interlocutory applications on the papers, and restricted discovery. The 
United Kingdom, in Part 28 of its Code of Civil Procedure, outl ines a fast track process that 
can be followed by the regular Courts. The procedure to be foll owed here emphasises the 
arrangements to be made prior to the trial itself, such as sett ing a timetable and listing out the 
evidence that will be submitted. The timetable is to ensure tha t the case is disposed of in a 
timely and efficient manner. Each country has their own set of fast track procedures and 
systems, however, the procedure and systems of the countries ca nnot be adopted in totality as 
Fast Track Courts in other jurisdictions are for civil cases an d FTSCs in India deals with 
criminal cases. 
 
3.23 However, this department has recommended a disposal plan f o r  t h e  F T S C s  t o  b e  
followed. Each FTSC is expected to dispose of, 41-42 cases in e ach quarter and at least 165 
cases in a year in order to remove the pendency. As on 31.03.20 22, 722 FTSCs including 406 
e-POCSO have been made functional in 28 States/UTs which have d isposed of more than 
87,100 cases since their inception. 
 
 

27 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.24 The Committee takes note of the reply. There is a need to revamp the FTSCs in 
accordance with the recommendations of the 'Third Part Party Ev aluation' referred 
above and the disposal plan for the FTSCs suggested by the Depa rtment. These reforms 
should be implemented and monitored on continuous basis in orde r to make these 
Courts truly 'fast track'.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.25 NALSA has recently completed 25 years of its establishment , accordingly, it is also 
the right time to ponder over reforms which are required in NAL SA and legal aid movement 
in India. Majority of Indians are eligible to receive legal aid , but the number of people 
actually receiving legal aid is a miniscule percentage of those  entitled. In the previous 
chapter, the Committee has already recommended a significant in crease in NALSA's budget 
and expects NALSA to make best use of it in performing its assigned mandate. (3.33) 
Action Taken 
 
3.26 It has been informed by NALSA that although majority of In dians are eligible to 
receive legal aid, only minuscule percentage of those entitled are actually availing the 
services provided by Legal Services Authorities, since a large number of categories are 
eligible even without application of means test. 
 
3.27 It has been further informed by NALSA that the National Me et of SLSAs is proposed 
to be organized shortly, wherein Hon’ble  Executive Chairperson s  o f  S t a t e  L e g a l  S e r v i c e s  
Authorities and Ld. Member Secretaries of State Legal Services Authorities will also 
participate with Central Authority i.e. NALSA, and will discuss  the issues pertaining to court 
based legal services i.e. Strengthening Front Offices as One St op Centre , Free Legal Aid, 
Advice, Counselling, Legal Aid Defence Counsel System, Legal As sistance at Pre-Arrest, 
Arrest and Remand Stages, Legal Aid To Prisoners, Pro Bono Lega l Services etc. will be 
deliberated and the strategy and methodology will be prepared. 
 
3.28 Strengthening Legal Services Institutions at grassroot lev el always remains the 
priority area and NALSA is focusing on several measures includi ng but not limited to 
following:  
 
1. People Centric Approach
: Work on “Beneficiary (Litigant) First Approach”, which 
w i l l  p l a c e  t h e  l i t i g a n t  a t  t h e  c e n t r e  o f  l e g a l  s e r v i c e  p r o v i s i on. NALSA will ensure 
increased monitoring and evaluation of legal services, in order  t o  e n s u r e  t h a t  m o r e  
effective and competent services are provided to meet the expec tations of legal aid 
beneficiary. 
 
2. One Nation-One DLSA : NALSA has already issued Regulations and SOPs for Pan 
India uniformity but still it is felt that more clearer and ela borative business rules are 
required for grassroot level district authority thus Uniform ru le of business in all 
District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) is need of the hour  a n d  N A L S A  i s  

28 
 
working over the same. Improvised processes to be incorporated to increase the 
outreach and legal literacy initiatives, for increasing vibrancy for legal services. 
 
3. Use of Digital Platform : Use of AI and digital platform from top to bottom for 
deliverable services as well as for monitoring quality of servi ce will be put in place 
during current year. An ODR platform for Pre-Institution Mediat ion (PIM) in 
commercial matters and also for all other Mediations in court a nnexed ADR/ 
Mediation centres of Legal services institutions will be launch ed soon, which will be 
first Online dispute resolution (ODR) platform in Government se ctor. We have 
already facilitated online filing of application for commercial  mediation through 
NALSA mobile App and portal in 10 languages. NALSA is already i n deliberations 
with NIC for a robust monitoring platform for accountability and efficiency.  
 
 In the period of turbulence caused by the COVID pandemic, Lega l Services 
Authorities appropriately responded by creatively adapting to t he new normal and 
successfully moved the conventional Lok Adalat to the virtual p latform enabling 
doorstep delivery of justice to common man. 
 
4. Incremental Expansion of Legal Aid Defence Counsel System:
 After successfully 
running the pilot project of Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (LADCS) at 13 places 
in 13 States, the Committee, constituted by the Central Authority has recommended to 
adopt full time lawyers engagement system for providing qualita tive and competent 
legal services to poor, marginalised and needy after comparing with counsel 
assignment system (Panel Lawyers scheme) at DLSA level. This sy stem is in line 
with Public defender system and will be fully operationalized i n  c u r r e n t  y e a r  i n  
following manner: 
 
i. 250 places (HQ- as per selection & availability of space) lates t by 15
th 
August 2022, 
ii. 250 more places (HQ) latest by 9th November 2022, 
iii. Remaining 200 District/ Judicial HQs by 26th January 2023. 
 
 At Outline or Taluka or sub-divisional places, which are not s eat of Principal District 
& Session Judge, existing Panel Lawyer (Counsel assignment) sys tem will continue 
with modified scheme.  
 
5. NALSA’s Early Access to Justice & Effective Legal Aid for inmat es:
 Effective 
implementation of NALSA's Early Access to Justice at Pre-Arrest , Arrest and 
Remand stage across the country. Further NALSA will conduct reg ular campaigns on 
mission mode basis for timely release of jail inmates. NALSA wi ll conduct regular 
campaigns on mission mode basis for timely release of jail inma tes. Increased focus 
on provision of legal services within the Juvenile Justice Mechanism. 
 
6. Integrity Code for Panel Lawyers:  As far as harassment of beneficiaries and demand 
of fee by panel lawyers is concerned, NALSA is already consider ing issuance of 
integrity code for legal aid lawyers. Even in upcoming SOPs pro visions for timely 

29 
 
interaction and filing timeline is also proposed. This Integrit y code for panel lawyers, 
in legal aid matters, will ensure adherence with professional standards and ethics. 
 
7. More vibrancy in Lok Adalat:  NALSA is committed to deliver prompt and 
inexpensive justice to the citizens and it has decided to lay m ore emphasis on 
contribution of National Lok Adal at in effectively reducing the  number of pending 
cases through Alternative Dispute Mechanisms. Lok Adalats are one of the most 
effective and successful Alternative Disputes Resolution mechan ism. The Lok Adalat 
has jurisdiction to take up any civil matters and all criminal compoundable matters 
which is either pending before any court or which has yet not b een brought to the 
court. In the year 2021, a total number of 1.27 crore cases hav e been settled in 4 
National Lok Adalat and out of which 55 Lakhs cases were alread y pending before 
the Courts of the country. It is proposed to further strengthen the Lok Adalats. 
 
3.29 However, there are certain challenges for NALSA, in streng thening the Legal 
Services Institutions at grassroots level and some of them are: -   
 
1. Strengthening of Legal Services Institutions at Grassroot level :
 There are 673 Legal 
Services Institutions at the District level. Section 9 (3) of t h e  L e g a l  S e r v i c e s  
Authorities Act, 1987 provides that the State Authority, in con sultation with the 
Chairman of the District Authority, appoint a person belonging to the State Judicial 
Service not lower in the rank than that of a subordinate Judge or Civil Judge as 
Secretary of the District Authority. Section 9 (5) of the Legal  Services Authorities 
Act, 1987 provides that the District Authority may appoint such  number of officers 
and other employees as may be prescribed by the State Governmen t in consultation 
with the Chief Justice of High Court for the efficient discharge of its functions. 
 
 Section 9 (7) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 prov ides that the 
administrative expenses of every District Authority, including the salaries, allowances 
and pensions payable to the Secretary, officers and other emplo yees of the District 
Authority shall be defrayed out of the Consolidated Fund of the  State. Out of 673 
District Legal Services Authorities, in 102 DLSAs, part time Se cretaries have been 
posted/appointed. The posts of the Secretary in all the DLSAs n eed to be created by 
the State Government and full time Secretaries have to be appoi nted in the remaining 
DLSAs. More over fix tenure is required for the Secretary, DLSAs.  
 
2. Inadequate support for State and District Legal Services Author ities by the State/UTs 
Governments: There is lack of staff and infrastructure in the State Legal Services 
Authorities and District Legal Services Authorities. Therefore,  to discharge the 
functions of the SLSAs and DLSAs, sufficient human resources ar e required to be 
deputed in the Legal Services Institutions. It is the statutory  duty of the State and UT 
Governments to create the necessary posts for the SLSA and DLSA s and to provide 
funds for administrative expenses  of the Legal Services Institu tions in the State for 
creation of proper infrastructure. It is submitted that barring  few States, most of the 
States/UTs are not supporting State/Legal Services Authorities with proper structural 
organisation framework. 

30 
 
 
3. Inadequate funds for victim compensation and non-adoption of NA LSA VCS for 
women survivors :      U n d e r  s e c t i o n  357-A of Cr PC, the operation of the Victim 
Compensation scheme is with the Legal Services Authorities and states have framed 
their schemes in pursuant to the provision. In case of Nipun Sa xena vs UOI, on the 
directions of Hon’ble Supreme Court, NALSA has prepared a victi m compensation 
scheme in 2018 for women survivors which is available on NALSA’ s website 
(enclosed for ready reference). This scheme is applicable to th e POCSO victims as 
well because there is no separate scheme for POCSO victims. There are two issues:- 
 
a. Adequate fund is not provided for victim compensation, so large  number of 
victims are not paid. 
b. A good number of states have not adopted NALSA Model Scheme, so  the victims 
are not getting adequate compensation. 
Further Observation 
3.30 The Central and State Governments are duty bound constitut ionally, legally and 
morally to ensure "access to justice for all". However, the ser iousness and attention 
from the various stakeholders of the legal aid movement is rath er missing. None other 
than the CJI has opined that the legal aid services are neglect ed in our country. So it is 
high time to pay adequate attention and seriousness to the lega l aid movement in India 
it deserves. State/UT Governments are equal partners in extending the legal aid services 
t o  t h e  e l i g i b l e  p o p u l a t i o n .  A s  i n f o r m e d  b y  N A L S A  t h e  i n f r a s t r u cture and manpower 
requirements at the grassroots levels are awfully inadequate. T hus the DoJ and NALSA 
are expected to have an effective consultation with the SLSAs a nd State/UT 
Governments and to impress upon them to provide all necessary i nfrastructure and 
manpower in order to provide a decent quality of legal aid to the people at grassroots.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.31 The Committee observes that the majority of the funds for NALSA are utilized for 
administrative services, rather than providing legal aid. Also,  p a n e l  l a w y e r s  a r e  n o t  b e i n g  
adequately compensated and their remuneration has remained stag nant for long. This affects 
the quality of legal aid service provided to the clients. This also often leads to lawyers found 
harassing beneficiaries or demanding ‘fees’ from them. The Comm ittee accordingly, 
recommends NALSA to compensate lawyers adequately, so that they  are able to sustain 
themselves and remain motivated in their job. On other hand, a robust system of monitoring 
the efficacy and accountability of legal aid services provided to the beneficiaries should also 
be put in place by NALSA. (3.34)  
Action Taken 
 
3.32 It is submitted that after observation of the Hon’ble Comm ittee regarding utilization 
of majority of funds for administrative services, a set of guid elines for spending funds have 
been issued by NALSA after obtaining with the approval of Hon’b le Executive Chairman, 
NALSA. 
 

31 
 
3.33 Regarding remuneration and adequate compensation to Panel Lawyers, it is submitted 
that after the resolution in Chief Justices and Chief Ministers  Conference – 2016, the 
State/UTs have taken note of the same and most of the States ar e paying as per 
recommendations of NALSA. In the year 2019, monthly remuneratio n (Retainer fee) of 
retainer lawyers have been increased across the country. Further, this issue will be taken up in 
the National Meet proposed to be organized shortly. 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.34 It is an undeniable fact tha t a majority of the people who are entitled to free legal 
aid see it as an option only when they cannot afford a private lawyer. The reason behind 
this is the lack of trust on the Legal Aid Counsels (LACs). The  q u a l i t y  o f  l e g a l  
representation and lack of commitment of the LACs towards the b eneficiary's case is a 
matter of concern. Quite often the LACs are meagerly paid and they are engaged on ad-
hoc basis. Thus there is a dire need to provide adequate remune ration to them and to 
revise it on regular basis. Further, appointing them on full ti me basis will certainly 
going to improve the level of commitment amongst the LACs.

POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.2 The Committee notes that even after 12 years of its separat ion from the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and becoming an independent Department, the Depart ment of Justice is still 
dependent on the MHA for all its man power requirements. The va cancies in the Department 
are particularly staggering at the middle and operating level o f SO, ASO (50% vacancy), 
UDC (100% vacancy), PA (100% vacancy) and Steno (100% vacancy).   It is surprising that 
the DoPT is posting officers of the rank of US and above direct ly to the Department, but 
other officials are posted by the MHA. There is hardly any just ification for this type of 
cumbersome arrangement being followed in the case of the Depart ment of Justice, where it is 
being given a step-motherly treatment in this matter. The Depar tment of Justice has been 
mandated with a significant role in appointment of judges, acce ss to justice and justice 
delivery. Accordingly, it should be provided with sufficient re sources and manpower to fulfil 
its mandate. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Depa rtment of Justice should be 
given full autonomy in case of personnel management and all cad re controlling authorities, 
including DoPT, should post all encadred posts directly to the Department of Justice. The 
Department of Justice is directed to bring this recommendation o f  t h e  C o m m i t t e e  t o  t h e  
notice of DoPT and MHA. (3.2)

                                   CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee observes that this Department is involved in examining new 
legislations for different Minis tries/Departments and also for repealing of obsolete laws. The 
Committee in its 101
st Report on Demands for Grants (2020-21) had made observations w ith 
regard to drafting errors and ambiguity in law/statutes and des ired for pre-legislative 
consultation and periodic review of legislations.  The Committe e is of the view that 
legislation enacted are not able to keep pace with changing soc io-economic developments 
leading to excessive litigations, financial loss to exchequer, disconnect with social milieu and 
so forth. (Para 3.15) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.15, it is to mention that:  
i. The process of legislation involves the study of social and financial costs, benefits and 
the key challenges that required to be settled before undertaki ng the legislations. The 
administrative Ministry/Department also identifies the problems  in the policy that 
needs to be addressed, the options it has considered and the re asons thereof in 
bringing forward a legislation.  
ii. Further, the Chapter 9 of the Manual of Parliamentary Procedure  in the Government 
of India (relating to legislation) provides that the concerned Ministry/Department has 
to formulate the legislative proposals in consultation with the  interested persons and 
authorities concerned, including holding discussions on the nec essity for the proposed 
legislation and on all matters of substance to be embodied therein. 
iii. Moreover, as per the Government of India (Allocation of Busines s) Rules, 1961, 
different subject matter or policies are allocated to different Ministries/Departments of 
the Government of India. Accordingly, the Ministries/Department s concerned with 
the subject matter initiates pre-legislative Consultations, hol ds deliberations with the 
public and all stakeholders and on that basis, finalise its leg islative policy and 
subsequently conduct the impact assessment after the legislations is enacted.  
iv. It is further pertinent to mention here that the Legislative De partment prepares draft 
laws in consultation with the administrative Ministry concerned  in accordance with 
the procedure laid down in the Manual of Parliamentary Procedur es, ordinarily within 
thirty days from the date of receipt of the proposal and after clearance from the 
Department of Legal Affairs. The refore, the Legislative Departm ent is merely a 
service provider Department catering its drafting services to t he 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India.  
 
Further Observation 
1.2 The Committee notes the Reply of the Department.

                                  CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE 
GOVERNMENT             
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The Committee desires that a general consensus is required on the issue of Legislative 
Impact Assessment (LIA), and accordingly of the considered view that there has to be a nodal 
Ministry/Department for dealing with the issues related to LIA,  and believes that the 
Legislative Department, due to its expertise in legislative/cab inet note drafting is the most 
suitable Department under the Government of India for the purpo se. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Department to prepare a white paper  on the Legislative Impact 
Assessment in the country by taking learning experiences of oth er developed countries. (Para 
3.16) 
Action Taken 
2.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.16, it is to mention that:  
i. The Legislative Impact Assessment or Analysis is a transparent and informed process 
with the participation and involvement of all stakeholders so that the preparedness and 
availability of requisite administrative, financial and infrast ructural support for 
successful implementation of intended legislation is known befo re hand and the 
desired object can be achieved. 
ii. The Legislative Impact Assessment is wide enough to encompass w ithin its scope 
Judicial Impact Assessment, Social Impact Assessment, Financial Impact Assessment, 
Environment Impact Assessment, Employment Impact Assessment, etc.  
 Judicial Impact Assessment  helps in preserving Courts ability to keep pace 
with growing workload, ensures, adequate funding of Courts and improves 
administration of justice. 
 Social Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the socio-economic impact of 
legislation on people, particularly those from the economically  weaker section 
and marginalized section of society. 
 Financial Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the economic costs of 
proposed legislation.  
 Environment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the beneficial and 
adverse impact of new legislation on environment, optimization of natural 
resources, reducing or mitigating potential negative impacts an d achieving 
9

sustainable development.  
 Employment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating employment creation 
through proposed legislation. 
iii. A law is reviewed by the concerned Ministry/Department for exam ining its 
effectiveness and setting right m ischief, if any, created by su ch law on the basis of 
feedback, if any, received from the stakeholders and the other concerned persons, the 
data, if any, collected in this behalf, the comments/suggestion s, if any, received from 
the public, etc. Thereafter, the concerned Ministry/Department takes up necessary 
l e g i s l a t i v e  a c t i o n  e i t h e r  f o r  a m e n d m e n t  o r  r e p e a l  o f  t h e  l a w .  Post-enactment 
legislative impact assessment is also done by the Law Commissio n of India or such 
other body or commission set up specifically for such purpose, which is normally 
limited to the specific terms of reference. 
iv. Under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1 961, each 
Ministry/Department has been allocated subject matters on which  t h a t  
Ministry/Department initiates, possess and implements legislati ve proposals and also 
studies social, economic, environmental and judicial impact of such  legislative 
proposals. 
v. In view of the above, pre-legislative consultations, legislative impact assessment /post 
legislation consultation are within the domain of the concerned  Ministry/Department. 
Hence, the pre and post Legislative Impact Assessment should be  done by the 
concerned Ministry/Department which piloted the legislation. Th erefore, the subject 
matter relating to legislative impact assessment does not come under the purview of 
the allocation of work to Legislative-I Section of this Department. 
vi. However, the Committee is of view that there has to be a nodal Ministry/Department 
for dealing with the issue related to Legislative Impact Assess ment and believes that 
the Legislative Department possess the expertise in legislative /cabinet note drafting 
and therefore, Legislative Department is considered as most sui table Department for 
the purpose. In this regards, it is to state that as explained above the legislative impact 
assessment /post legislation consultation is a wide concept and  involves intricacies, 
specialized knowledge, expertise, manpower, research work and i nfrastructure and as 
the Legislative Department does not intervene in the policy mat ter of the legislation 
rather only provides its drafting services to the Ministries/De partments. In view of the 
a b o v e ,  L e g i s l a t i v e  D e p a r t m e n t  i s  e x a m i n i n g  v a r i o u s  a s p e c t s  r e l ating to the 
recommendation made by the Department related Parliamentary Sta nding Committee, 
and the manner of its implementation and suitable decision take n by the competent 
authority will be communicated in due course of time. 
 
Further Observation 
 
2.2 The committee acknowledges the reply of the department.

in Assamese, Bodo, Gujarati, Konkani, Kashmiri, Maithili, Nepal i, Odia, Santhali, 
Sanskrit and Sindhi and the current status of the such initiati ves may be forwarded for 
the perusal of the Committee. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.23 The Committee also observes that posts of language officer  are vacant for Assamese, 
Gujarati, Kanada, Odia, Urdu, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Konkani, Nepali  and Manipuri. Further, no 
post of language officers have been sanctioned for Bodo, Santha li, Maithali, Dogri and 
Kashmiri languages. The Committee is surprised to note that no post/s for language officers 
has been created in the Department for Kashmiri language (1950) , which was included in the 
Eighth Schedule more than 70 years ago. Further, even after 17 years of inclusion in the Eight 
Schedule, no posts of languages o fficers have been created for Bodo, Santhali, Maithali,  and 
Dogri, despite having large number of people speaking these Sch eduled Languages viz. 
Maithali ( 12,179,122), Santhali (6,469,600), Kashmiri (5,527,6 98), Dogri (2,282,589), and 
Bodo (1,350,478). The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department not only to fill-
up the vacant position of language officers in the Department  and also approach appropriate 
authorities for creating posts of language officers for Bodo, S anthali, Maithali, Dogri and 
Kasmiri languages without any further delay. (Para 3.12) 
Action Taken 
 
3.24 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.12, Offic ial Language Wing 
(OLW) has submitted that the recruitment rules for the post of Group ‘A’ Officer (Regional 
Languages) are under consideration. It is mentioned that there is no post sanctioned for Bodo, 
Maithali, Dogri and Kasmiri languages. As per records, there is  already a sanctioned post for 
16

the Santhali language. It is submitted that necessary action wi ll be taken up with the 
concerned authorities for getting sanctioned posts for these fo ur languages viz. Bodo, 
Maithali, Dogri and Kasmiri. 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.25 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. The Commi ttee desires early 
action may be initiated for getting posts of the four language viz. Bodo, Maithali, Dogri 
and Kashmiri filled. The Department may apprise the Committee o f the action taken in 
this regard.

ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.0 The Committee observes that as against an allocation of Rs.  253.00 crore in the 
current Financial Year, the expenditure of the ECI till 31
st January, 2022 is only Rs. 158.74 
crore (63 percent approx.). The Committee observes that out of the total allocation of Rs. 
7.00 crore for capital expenditure in the current financial yea r; the ECI has not been able to 
spend a single rupee till 31 st January, 2022. The Committee understands that expenditure 
under the capital head is directly linked with the external age ncies like CPWD and NBCC for 
construction of building for ECI at Dwarka, however, the Committee  fails to understand why 
only Rs. 158.74 has been spent under the Revenue head which is well within the control of 
ECI, and accordingly, the Committee recommends ECI to furnish c ogent reasons for under-
utilisation of funds allocated to it under the Revenue head. (Para 2.17) 
     
4.1 The Committee also observes allocations have been reduced u nder Revenue heads- 
Information Technology, Voters’ Awareness, and Training of ECI,  w h i c h  t h e  C o m m i t t e e  
believes are important components of electoral processes. The Committee feels that reduction 
in allocations under the Revenue Expenditure for the forthcomin g financial year vis-à-vis 
projection to the Ministry of Finance may be due to the inabili ty of the ECI to spend the 
allocations made for various heads in the current financial year. (Para 2.18) 
 
4.2 The Committee, accordingly, recommends the ECI to improve i ts spending capacity 
on various activities, as non- expe nditure of amount allocated reflects under-performance of 
activities/under-utilisation of resources. The Committee is the refore of the view that an 
important institution like ECI should not be forced to limit it s activities due to financial 
constraints and recommends the Department/ECI to approach the M inistry of Finance for 
enhanced allocation during the RE stage, especially for Informa tion Technology and Voters’ 
Awareness and Training . (Para 2.19)

Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its One Hundred

Department of Legal Affairs (Ministry of Law & Justice), which was presented to

2. The Committee had made 30 recommendations/observations in its 11 5th 
Report. Replies of the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized 
under four chapters on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies 
have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations (7) which have be en accepted by 
the Department, i.e. in respect of paras 2.23, 3.15, 3.16, 3.19, 3.27, 
3.28 and 3.30 of the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that 
the Department has accepted those recommendations. 
Chapter – II:  Recommendations/observations (9) which the Committee does not 
desire to pursue in view of the replies given by the Department, i.e. 
in respect of paras 2.21, 2.22, 3.13, 3.22, 3.23, 3.38, 3.41, 3.42 and 
3.45 of the Report. The Committee is satisfied with the 
explanations advanced by the D epartment and does not wish to 
pursue those as of now.  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations (8) in respect of which Committee 
has not accepted the replies of the Department, i.e. with regard to 
paras 2.13, 2.14, 2.15, 2.17, 3.6, 3.7, 3.14, and 3.34 of the Report. 
The Committee does not accept the reasons given by the 
Department and reiterates the same. 
Chapter - IV: Recommendations/observations ( 6) in respect of which final 
replies of the Department have not been received, i.e. in respect of 
paras 3.52, 3.53, 3.54, 3.59, 3.60 and 3.61  of the Report, the 
Committee has not received replies.

detailed Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further 
Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in this report.

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE DEPARTMENT 
NEW DELHI INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION CENTRE (NDIAC) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee also observes that the Department has also not been able to spend a 
single rupee out of the funds allocated from the Financial Years 2020 -21 onwards; it has sought 
exponentially higher allocations. The Committe e, accordingly, recommends that the Department 
in future needs to rationally project its demand under the head NDIAC. (2.23) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 It is submitted that tentative provisions in the budget were made anticipating finalization 
of the establishment  of the NDIAC after completion of the requisite and ongoing procedural 
requirements. 
  
1.2 It is submitted that for enabling smooth and expeditious functioning of the NDIAC, the 
anticipated expenditure for which the funds had been solicited included ,setti ng up the 
Arbitration Centre, payment of salary and allowances to officers/officials of the Centre, likely 
expenditure on Rooms/work station of Chairman/Members and other officers/employees of 
NDIAC. Further, since the repair/maintenance of the building lo cated at Vasant Kunj, where the 
NDIAC would be functioning from, is also being undertaken by this Department through 
CPWD, certain budgetary projections were also made to meet expenditure on the maintenance of 
the aforesaid building. 
  
1.3 With the establishment of the Centre, vide notification dated 13.6.2022, the utilization of 
the funds for the Centre is expected to increase. It is further submitted that as advised by the 
Committee, the considered and rational budget estimates shall be prepared keeping i n view the 
likely expenditure towards operationalization and functioning of the NDIAC. 
 
Further observation 
 
1.4 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.5 The Committee further observes  that the distribution of notaries across the States/UTs is 
uneven and believes that there should be objective criteria to project required number of notaries 

 
10 
in States/UTs to optimally utilize their services. The Committee understands that notary -ship is 
not a civil post or any kind of employment under the Central Government and hence does not 
attract any affirmative policy in any manner. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the 
Department to make a wholehearted endeavour so that composition of notaries is inc lusive and 
reflects the balanced socio-economic composition of the society. (3.15) 
Action Taken 
1.6 In terms of provisions of Notaries Rules, 1956, only relaxations in terms of „ experience 
as an advocate/legal practitioner „ as eligibility condition are provided in favour of social 
category candidates  (SC/ST/OBC/Women/PH) ( seven years‟ experience vis a vis 10 years for 
general category candidates) . The prescribing of eligibility qualifications in terms of experience 
however do not mean any kind of social category reservations as such in favour of any of these 
categories in appointment of notaries.  
1.7 The schedule appended to the Notaries rules, 1956 provide details of maximum number 
of notaries to be appointed in the State/UT by the central Government as well as State 
Governments. The schedule is periodically amended in view of request made by the re spective 
State Governments for enhancement of their State/UT quota and same is considered on the 
criteria of (i) increase in the population of the concerned State/UT (ii) increase in the number of 
districts or tehsil or taluka of concerned State/UT. 
1.8 The central Government also enhance their quota for central government notaries on 
account of increase in number of Courts/Tribunals, creation of more districts /Talukas, increase 
in commercial activities in the State, industrialization, increase in number o f educational 
institutions and increase in population in the State. 
1.9 Accordingly, vacancies for notaries in particular State/UTs are determined on account of 
number of factors explained above. 
Further Observation 
 
1.10 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
 
DIGITAL SIGNATURES FOR AUTHENTICATION OF NOTARIZED DOCUMENTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.11 The Committee in its previous reports, including 101st, 107th and 109th Reports dealt the 
issue of digital signatures and had recommended the Department t o explore the feasibility of 
introducing Digital Signatures for authenticating notarized documents to reduce malpractices of 
anti-dating or/and attestation of blank document, etc. and improve transparency. The Committee 
also feels that along with digital s ignatures, the Department may also explore the feasibility of 

 
11 
introducing e -affidavits as practice of e -stamping is already in vogue and the Government of 
India is also promoting courts through video conferencing and virtual courts. (3.16) 
Action Taken 
 
1.12 The issue of introduction of digital signature facility for notary attestations has been 
examined. It is submitted that majority of the documents which are presented for notarization 
before a Notary Public are invariably in the physical form. Apart from  signature, a notary has to 
put his seal and also affix notarial stamp on the documents being notarized by him. Digital 
signature means „authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of any 
electronic method or procedure on the documents ‟. Using of digital signature for authentication 
of documents to be notarized by a Notary, such documents must be in electronic form whereas 
majority of such documents are invariably presented in physical form which are not compatible 
for Digital Signature. 
  
1.13 As regards introducing e -affidavits, the subject is not within the purview of the Notaries 
Act 1952 and rules framed thereunder.  
  
1.14 Thus, in present circumstances introducing digital signatures for authentication of 
documents on the part of Notary may not be viable. 
 
Further Observation 
 
1.15 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
EMPANELMENT OF COUNSELS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.16 The Committee observes that the Department has not devised any criteria/methodology to 
project the required number of panel counsels for a Court/ Tribunal. Further, there is no 
information available on the Department‟s website with regard to empanelment process of panel 
counsels. The Committee, accordingly, feels that the Department needs to devise a ra tional 
methodology for projecting required number of panel counsels/advocates based on the number of 
institution/pending cases, nature of cases and so forth to ensure transparency and optimal 
utilisation of government resources. The details of empanelment process/criteria also need to be 
uploaded in the Department‟s website for the benefit of potential candidates applying for 
empanelment as government/panel counsels. (3.19) 
Action Taken 
1.17 It is stated that the panel counsel for various courts / tribunals  are engaged by this 
Department to represent Union of India for a particular term and as such they are not appointed 
against any civil post. Therefore, the concept of sanctioned post or vacant posts does not apply in 

 
12 
case of panel counsel. Presently, there  is no criteria/methodology to project the required number 
of panel counsel for a court/tribunal. It is pertinent to mention here that relationship between a 
panel counsel & Government is that of an Advocate and client. Empanelment/engagement of 
Advocates to represent Government before various courts should not be compared with 
appointment to a “post” in the Government. There is no extra financial burden on the 
Government on empanelling large number of counsel as payment of fee is paid to them on case -
to-case basis in lieu of their professional services. Further, Government has more choices to 
choose/select suitable counsel from the panel in terms of expertise and experience required to 
defend a particular case.   However, keeping in view the size of the cour t, number of Central 
Govt. litigations etc. appropriate number of counsel are engaged for that court. Moreover, due to 
expiry of terms, deaths and resignation etc. of counsel, the process of empanelment/engagement 
of Advocates as panel counsel is an ongoin g process due to which projecting total number of 
panel counsel for a High Court on an earlier date is not feasible.   
1.18 Further, it is a settled proposition of law enunciated by the Hon‟ble Supreme Court of 
India and various High Courts that Government  Advocate being a special engagement has no 
vested right to continue in that position. Appointment of Government Advocate is purely a 
prerogative of the Government because it is a professional engagement between a litigant and its 
Advocate. As such, at pre sent, Advocates are empanelled / engaged by this Department for all 
courts/tribunals in the country with the approval of Hon‟ble Minister for Law & Justice and 
orders in this regard are issued on behalf of the President.   We may, therefore, publish this 
procedure on website of the Department for public information.  
Further Observation 
 
1.19 The Committee takes note of the reply.

BUDGET ALLOCATION TO INDIAN LAW INSTITUTE 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Department/ ILI  has informed that over the last 5 years, 100 percent of funds 
released to ILI have been utilised and there was excess expenditure (50 percent approx.) of ILI 
vis-à-vis grants allocated for the same period. The ILI has informed this Committee that it has 
incurred an expenditure of Rs. 6.7 crore in the current financial year (as on 31.1.2022) towards 
payment of salaries and allowances. However, the Committee observes that the ILI is not able to 
meet even its salary requirement for teaching and non -teaching staff from the grants allocated by 
the Department of Legal Affairs. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that ILI being a 
grantee institution should not eternally depend on government grants and thus it needs to become 
self sufficient to meet its basic r equirements. The Committee also feels that for the time being, 
grants-in-aid to ILI may be enhanced. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department 
to at least provide grants -in-aid to meet its 100 percent salary and allowances expenditure for 
sanctioned positions for the next five years. (2.13) 
3.1 The Committee observes that majority of earnings of ILI is from course fee charged from 
students/trainees, rent received from Ministry of Law and Justice for leasing its premises, and 
interests. The Committee also observes that the pattern of earning has remained same for the last 
2-3 years, except some variations in financial year 2020 -21 due to Covid -19 pandemic. The 
Committee is of the view that the ILI being a research Institution, needs to generate mo re and 
more funds from academic and consultancy activities, which are its core activities and not from 
rent/leasing its premises to Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the ILI to explore additional avenues to generate more funds from 
research/ consulting activities and gradually become self sufficient. (2.14) 
 
3.2 The Committee also feels that ILI needs to expand its activities by way of introducing 
demand degrees/diploma programmes and consultancy activitie s by optimally utilising its 
existing infrastructure and accordingly, is of the view that its premises rented out to the 
Departments/institutions needs to be utilised for its own expansion. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Department to get the ILI premises vacated for its expansion. (2.15)

Indian Law Institute (ILI) as Grants -in-Aid. Besides that Rs.6.50 crore has been provided to ILI

allowances, the proposal for enhancement of Grant -in-Aid (Salary) to Rs.6.00 crore has been 
agreed to by this Department and sent to Integrate d Finance Division for getting the same 
approved by the Competent Authority. 
3.4 ILI has informed that at present, the Institute manages to generate an amount of Rs.4.00 
crore through its own resources i.e. course fee, rent, sale of publications, research activities etc. 
Further, it is difficult for the Institute to introduce more academic courses due to space 
constraints and lack of infrastructure and there is very less scope for the Institute to earn more 
revenue from its core activities. However, the Ins titute is continuously striving to explore more 
avenues for expansion of its academic, research and consulting activities to generate more funds. 
3.5 The Indian Law Institute (ILI) building has been constructed with a loan from the 
Government with an agreement between the Government and ILI to rent out some portion of the 
building to the Government by the ILI. ILI has rented out 13184 Sq. Feet portion of the building 
to the Department of Legal Affairs. As per the recommendation of the committee, the 
Department of Legal Affairs may consider vacating the rented portion of the premises, for 
optimum utilization of the infrastructure of ILI, when the Central Vista made operational, 
accommodating all offices of the Department of Legal Affairs in the Central Vista. 
Further Observation  
3.6 The Indian Law Institute (ILI) was founded primarily with the objective of 
promoting and conducting legal research. After more than six decades of its coming into 
existence the institute is expected to  have evolved itself into a center of excellence in the 
field of Law. For this , the Government should provide adequate funds for running the 
institute and augmenting its infrastructure. On the other hand the ILI should generate 
more funds from research/consulting activ ities and gradually become self sufficient in 
terms of finances.  
ARBITRATION COUNCIL OF INDIA 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.7 The Committee observes that the Department was not able to spend a single Rupee from 
the allocations made under the head Arbitrat ion Council of India (ACI) in the Financial Year 
(2020-21) & (2021 -22), however, it has again made a projection of Rs. 6.50 crore for the 
Financial Year (2022 -23) to the Ministry of Finance, against which Rs. 3.00 crore has been 
allocated in BE (2022 -23). In view of the above, the Committee feels that submission of 
Department that ACI allocations is primarily due to judicious expenditure in the Financial Year 
2021-22 and projection of optimum budget requirement in Financial Year (2022 -23), is not 

 
26 
tenable. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to expedite the appointment 
process of Chairperson, Members and Secretariat Staffs without further delay so that it become s 
functional, and apprise the Committee about the timeline in this regard. (2.17)  
Action Taken 
 
3.8 It is submitted that tentative provisions in the budget for ACI were made anticipating 
establishment of the ACI after completion of the requisite and ongoing procedural requirements. 
  
3.9 As regards the steps taken for enabling establishment of the ACI, it is submitted that after 
consultation with the concerned Departments, the following Rules have been framed and notified 
pursuant to the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019 and also laid before the 
both Houses of the Parliament during the Monsoon Session of Parliament (In the Rajya Sabha on 
28.07.2022 and in Lok Sabha on 29.07.2022).

3.10 Further, during deliberations and discussions regarding establishment of ACI, it emerged 
that as ACI has been envisaged as an autonomous body, funding of the ACI directly through a 
direct budget line may not be possible. Therefore, provisions are required to be made in the 
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 for funds and grants for ACI.  Moreover,  since  the  ACI  
would  be  fully  funded  by  the  Central Government, provisions are required to be provided in 
the Act for audit of the accounts of the ACI to be carried out by CAG and the related aspects. 
  
To enable inclusion of the requisite provisions relating to ACI as afore mentioned, the 
Department has taken steps to carry out the requisite amendments to the Arbitration and 
Conciliation Act, 1996. It is proposed to introduce the said amendment in the Parliament in the 
ensuing session. 
  

 
27 
3.11 Upon the amendments being carried  and enabling provisions being introduced, further 
expeditious and immediate steps for establishment and operationalization of the ACI would be 
taken. 
Further observation  
 
3.12 The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was amended by the Arbitration and 
Conciliation (Amendment) Act 2019 and certain provisions of the Amendment Act were 
enforced w.e.f 30.08.2019. The said Amendment Act inter -alia provided for the 
establishment and incorporation of an independent body namely, the Arbitration Council 
of India  (ACI) for the purpose of grading of arbitral institutions and accreditation of 
arbitrators, etc. Subsequently, the Government has also notified 4 rules in connection with 
the establishment of the ACI. However, the Department is now stating that there is a  
requirement to further amend the 1996 Act for incorporating provisions related to funding 
of the ACI. The Committee accordingly, recommends the Government to bring the 
requisite amendment at the earliest and make the ACI fully functional at the earliest. 
 
VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.13 The Committee observes that around 50 percent of Indian Legal Service posts, as 
compared to sanctioned posts, are vacant at various grades. Further, large number of posts of 
General Central Services (GCS), Central Secretariat Services (CSS), Central Secret ariat 
Stenographer Services (CSSS), Central Secretariat Clerical Services (CSCS), and Central 
Secretariat Official Language Service (CSOLS) are also vacant in the Department. The 
Department has informed that in consultation with recruiting agencies like UP SC and SSC and 
cadre controlling authority DoPT, various processes have been initiated to fill -up these vacancy 
positions. The Committee in its previous reports on Demands for Grants had also raised the issue 
of vacancy positions in the Department and acco rdingly, had pointed that filling -up of these 
vacancies positions need to be expedited for smooth functioning of the Department. (3.6)  
3.14 The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to approach the concerned 
cadre controlling and recruiting agencies, i.e. Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), 
Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and Staff Selection Commission (SSC), and impress 
upon them to fill -up the vacancy positions of General Central Services (GCS), Central 
Secretariat Services (CSS), Central Secretariat Stenographer Services (CSSS), Central 
Secretariat Clerical Services (CSCS), and Central Secretariat Official Language Service 
(CSOLS) officers. The Committee further recommends the Department to at least fill -up 
vacancies of ILS Officers in a time bound manner, as the Department of Legal Affairs itself is 
the cadre controlling authority of this service. (3.7) 
 
 

 
28 
Action Taken 
 
3.15 The vacancies in various grades belonging to the Cadres of Central Secretariat Services 
(CSS), Central Secretariat Stenographer Services (CSSS), Central Secretariat Clerical Services 
(CSCS), and Central Secretariat Official Language Services (CSOLS) are filled up on the basis 
of nomination received from the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) and Department of 
Official Language (DoOL) respectively. 
3.16 The shortage of manpower in the posts belonging to above mentioned cadres is due to 
non-receipt of nominations from DoPT and DoOL in spite of repeated reminders. The vacancies 
in the grades of Accounta nt and Junior Accountant belonging to General Central Service (GCS) 
Cadre could not be filled up as the Recruitment Rules of these posts are being amended.  
3.17 Matter is being taken up with DoPT and DoOL regularly for making nominations against 
the vacan t posts. Latest reminder in this regard was sent on 30.08.2022 and 01.08.2022 
respectively. Efforts are being made to finalize the process of amendment of Recruitments Rules 
in respect of the posts of Accountant and Junior Accountant at the earliest. 
 3.18 As regards GCS Cadre in the Department of Legal Affairs, vacancies have already been 
reported to the SSC for 10 posts of Court Clerks to be appointed through Direct Recruitment    
and 13 of Court Clerks have been reported for Limited Departmental Competiti ve Examination.  
Further, SSC has recommended 11 candidates for the posts of Assistant Legal and all candidates 
have joined the department. Status regarding Action Taken for filling up the posts in Legal 
Adviser Cadre and Government Advocate Cadre as on 10.06.2022 may be seen at Annexure-A .  
Further observation 
 
3.19 Shortage of manpower  has been a perennial  problem in the Department of Legal 
Affairs notably in the Indian Legal Service (ILS) cadre, who are the Principal Legal 
Advisers to the Government. The Committee in its p revious reports has time and again 
recommended accelerating the recruitment process for ILS b ut the Department citing 
delays in amending the Recruitment Rules (RRs), Court Cases etc. has lagged behind in 
overcoming the shortage, which presently is about 50% of the cadre strength. As the ILS 
cadre play a pivotal role in the functioning of the Depar tment of Legal Affairs and 
Legislative Department, the Committee once again recommends the Government to fill all 
the pending vacancies in the ILS cadre on priority and overcome all the hurdles in 
achieving this target. A time line for filling up of all vacancies in the cadre may be prepared 
and shared with the Committee. 
3.20 As far as vacancies in the CSS, CSSS, CSCS and CSOL cadre are concerned the 
Department should take up the matter with the concerned cadre controlling authorities 
from higher level and with more vigor, rather than shooting an innocent reminder to them 
on regular basis. 
 

 
29 
VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
3.21 The Committee also observes that from the year 2019 onwards very few appointments 
i.e. 2019(439), 2020(0), and 2 021(91) have been made by the Department despite large number 
of vacant positions and more than 81000 pending online applications. The Committee is not 
convinced with the submission of the Department that appointment could not be made due to 
covid-19 pandemic, as prior to the covid -19 pandemic also large number of positions of notaries 
were vacant in various States/UTs. Further, in the year 2019, when there was no covid -19 
pandemic, very few appointments of notaries were made. The Committee feels that the 
Department needs to make an all out effort to fill -up the vacant positions and accordingly, 
recommends the Department to submit a status note proposing a tentative timeline for filling 
these vacant posts while furnishing Action Taken Replies. The Committee,  further, recommends 
the Department to publish names of officers along with contact details dealing with notaries in its 
website for the benefit of notary applicants and general public. (3.14) 
Action Taken 
3.22 In the year 2018 and 2019, number of intervie w Boards for conducting interviews in 
various States/UTs were constituted. However, due to Covind -19 Pandemic, no interviews could 
be conducted in any of States/UTs in the year 2020-21, except in the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir 
where interviews were conducted in the month of September, 2021 and 91 candidates have been 
appointed. Further, interviews for the UT of Puducherry have also been completed. Furthermore, 
process is over for the state of Himachal Pradesh.   
3.23 In view of non -conducting of interviews du e to Covid -19 Pandemic, online applications 
from all the States/UTs have been received and Notary Cell has accordingly decided to increase 
the number of vacancies for central government notaries in these States/UTs. A Gazette 
notification to this effect h as been issued. The notification paves the way for holding of 
interviews in these States/UTs in phased manner as decided by the Central Government. 
3.24 Furthermore in 09 States including North Eastern States, advertisements have been issued 
in local newspapers inviting Online Notary Applications with last date as 31st July, 2022. The 
last date for inviting applications in these States were further extended till 31st August, 2022.  
3.25 Names and Designation of Officers and Staff along with contact det ails working in 
Notary Cell have been published on the official website of the Department. 
Further Observation  
3.26 As per the data provided by the Department about two -third of vacancies of 
Notaries in the country has remained unfilled as on 31.12.2021. Even before the onset of 
COVID there were huge vacancies of Notaries in the country. The pandemic has caused 

 
30 
further delay in appointment. Since, t he effects of the pandemic has almost completely 
waned, the Department should set a time-line to fill up the vacancies of Notaries.  
 
INDIAN LAW INSTITUTE (ILI) 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.27 The Committee observes that out of the sanctioned 20 teaching posts, only 7 posts (35 
percent) are filled-up. Further, out of 75 non teaching posts, only 36 are in position (48 Percent). 
The Committee is not convinced with the argument of the ILI that existing strength of teaching 
and non -teaching posts is sufficient to meet the present requirement and is of the unanimous 
view that for the ILI t o function at its optimal level, it will have to fill -up the vacant positions of 
teaching and non -teaching staffs. The Committee also feels that ILI may explore the feasibility 
of introducing post -doctoral research fellowships to young legal researchers on  emerging legal 
areas. (3.34) 
Action Taken 
3.28 It is submitted that the Department has increased the grant to Indian law Institute (ILI) by 
Rs.1.00 crore under „Salary and allowance” head  to an amount of Rs.3.50 crore in R.E 2021 -22 
from Rs 2.50 crore all ocation in BE -2021-22.   However, although under BE 2022 -23 the 
allocation under “Grants -in-Aid Salaries” has been kept to Rs.3.00 crore, the Department has 
noted the recommendation of the Committee regarding enhancement of budget under this head, 
and the matter shall be taken up with the Department of Expenditure to increase allocation under 
“Grants-in-Aid Salaries” head to ILI during RE 2022-23 on the basis of demand of ILI.   
3.29 The ILI has also been advised to take action to implement the recommendati on of the 
Committee regarding exploring the feasibility of introducing post -doctoral research fellowships 
to young legal researchers on emerging legal areas.  
Further Observation 
 
3.30 It seems that the teaching positions and other posts have been kept vac ant due to 
want of sufficient funds for giving salaries and allowances. The Committee feels saddened 
to note that an institution of the stature of ILI is made to run with 35% of the sanctioned 
teaching posts due to dearth of funds. The Committee wants to s ee the ILI to expand and 
prosper; not to shrink and stagnate. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the 
Government to support ILI whole-heartedly with funds and otherwise, for its development 
and expansion, so that it lives upto its mandate and expectation.

31

FINAL REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
 
BAR COUNCIL OF INDIA 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4.0 The Committee observes from the submissions made by both the Department of Legal 
Affairs and Bar Council of India that the Department releases grants only after receiving request 
from concerned organisa tion/Institution and no such application for seeking grants has been 
received from the BCI, hence there is no proposal for release of Grants to BCI by the 
Department. The Committee was apprised of the plight of lawyers due to covid -19 pandemic by 
BCI and i nfrastructural constraints of Bar Councils/Associations and request for recommending 
grants, including provisions for medical aid, health insurance etc. to undertake welfare activities.  
(3.52) 
Action Taken 
4.1 Reply from Implementation Cell, Department of Legal Affairs on the recommendations 
related to Bar Council of India (BCI) is still awaited and the same would be submitted as soon as 
the response / inputs are received from Implementation Cell / BCI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4.2 The Committee observes from the submission of the BCI that many Bar Associations, 
especially in rural areas require proper infrastructure and basic amenities like toilets, drinking 
water, fans, good library for facilitating good practice of Advocacy, compu ters with internet 
facilities and proper sitting space for Advocates and their clients, and is of the view that without 
a conducive atmosphere, the justice system suffers and leads to delays and pendency of cases. 
The Committee feels that BCI needs to be p rovided with some grants by the Department for 
basic infrastructural and other facilities like sitting space, clean drinking water, electricity, 
libraries, etc. in various courts, and accordingly, recommends the Bar Council of India to 
approach the Department of Legal Affairs for Grants -in –aid. The Committee also feels that the 
Department may approach the Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice for exploring 
the feasibility of recommending grants/or including infrastructure facilities for Bar As sociations 
under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for 
Districts and Subordinate Judiciary. The Committee, further, recommends the Department of 
Legal Affairs to explore the feasibility of providing grants to  the BCI and also submit a status 
note to this Committee while furnishing Action Taken Replies on the issue along with 
appropriate justifications. (3.53)  

 
32 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.3 Reply from Implementation Cell, Department of Legal Affairs on the recommendations  
related to Bar Council of India (BCI) is still awaited and the same would be submitted as soon as 
the response / inputs are received from Implementation Cell / BCI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4.4 The Committee also feels that budgetary allocations for W elfare of Advocates during 
pandemic and natural calamities may be made in the budget allocation, and there should also be 
provisions to disburse interest free /low interest loans. It also feels that that there is a requirement 
for life/term insurance and h ealth insurance as well as for nominal/subsidized medical facilities 
for majority of Advocates and their families, who are under financial duress, more so, due to the 
pandemic. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to explore available 
options and modalities in this regard and submit a status note while submitting the action taken 
replies. (3.54) 
Action Taken 
4.5 Reply may be sent while received from Bar Council of India/ Implementation Cell, 
Department of Legal Affairs. 
Recommendation/Observation  
4.6 The Committee appreciates the Bar Council of India‟s initiative to improve the standards 
of legal education, however, it is of the view that utmost care must be taken in granting 
recognition to law colleges/institutions to impart legal educatio n across the country. The 
Committee observes that legal education is being commercialized and many colleges without 
having proper class room, building, library etc. and ghost teachers are granting law degrees and 
candidates without attending law classes ar e enrolling as advocates thereby increasing the pool 
of sub-standard lawyers. (3.59) 
Action Taken 
4.7 Reply from Implementation Cell, Department of Legal Affairs on the recommendations 
related to Bar Council of India (BCI) is still awaited and the same wou ld be submitted as soon as 
the response / inputs are received from Implementation Cell / BCI. 
 Recommendation/Observation  
4.8 The Committee also feels that the BCI also needs to improve the standard of All India 
Bar Examinations (AIBE) and accordingly rec ommends that exit examination to practice law in 
the country should be made compulsory without any further relaxations. Further, the Committee 

 
33 
is of the strong view that to enhance the quality of legal education and preserve the credibility of 
legal profes sion, the BCI needs to improve its regulatory functions and therefore, law 
universities promoting malpractices needs to be strictly dealt with. (3.60) 
Action Taken 
4.9 Reply from Implementation Cell, Department of Legal Affairs on the recommendations 
related to Bar Council of India (BCI) is still awaited and the same would be submitted as soon as 
the response / inputs are received from Implementation Cell / BCI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4.10 The Committee also feels that as part of improving the legal education and profession in 
the country, the BCI may explore the options of revisiting the earlier practice of compulsory 
apprenticeship of law graduates, and Department/BCI should apprise the Committee about their 
considered opinion on the issue. (3.61) 
Action Taken 
4.11 Reply from Implementation Cell, Department of Legal Affairs on the recommendations 
related to Bar Council of India (BCI) is still awaited and the same would be submitted as soon as 
the response / inputs are received from Implementation Cell / BCI. 
 
Further Observation 
 
4.12 The Committee notes that ATR has not been received from the BCI/Implementation 
Cell even after elapse of sufficient time given to them. The Department should impress 
upon the BCI/Implementation Cell to furnish the ATR on  the recommendations of the 
Committee, immediately, without any further delay.

CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND 
TRAINING 
Introduction 
1.0. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the nodal 
Ministry for matters relating to personnel management in the Government of India. 
1.1. The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T) 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) 
(iii) Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DPPW) 
 
 
1.2. The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Hon‘ble Prime 
Minister assisted by the Minister of State. The Department of Personnel and Training 
is functioning under the charge of a Secretary. 
1.3. Department of Personnel and Training formulates policies concerning 
recruitment, training, career progression, staff welfare and the post-retirement 
dispensation.  
Divisions of DoPT:  
1.4 Various wings of DoPT are as under:
