3.5 The Committee appreciates the 10-step CPGRAMS reforms process that was 
adopted by DARPG for improving quality of disposal and reducing the time lines. The 
Committee also commends the Department for the faster rate of disposal of grievances 
by the Department which is over one lakh per month. But the Committee is of the view 
that 'Quality of Grievance Redressal' is more important rather than 'Quantity of 
Grievance Disposal' and therefore, recommends the Department to focus more on 
'Redressal' of grievances as compared to 'Disposal' of grievances.   
3.6 The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has implemented most of 
its recommendations like One Nation One Portal, CPGRAMS portal in all Regional 
Languages, to develop Grievance Redressal Index, reduction in redressal period from 
60 to 45 days and 45 to 30 days, introduction of appellate mechanism, revamping of 
Sevottam Scheme, operationalising of Feedback mechanism and CPGRAMS 
Dashboard. The Committee, therefore, appreciates and commends the efforts of the 
Department for continuously improving and bringing about thoughtful changes in the 
grievance redressal system.  
3.7   The Committee on a recent study visit to Imphal, Guwahati and Agartala 
identified 'Strengthening of Public Grievance Redressal System' as one of the subjects 
for discussion with the officials of State Governments. The Committee observed that the 
system of grievance redressal in North-Eastern states is not very robust and needs 
considerable improvement. Also in its written replies the Department has informed the 
Committee that there is no separate State Grievance Portal in any of North-Eastern 
state except Meghalaya. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to aid 
these states to develop an efficient separate State Grievance portal and also link it with 
CPGRAMS portal for proper monitoring. The Committee also recommends the 
Department to formulate a policy focussing on North-Eastern states so that Public 
Grievance Redressal System in these States can be ameliorated.  
3.8 The Committee observes that whereas the number of disposal of Grievance 
redressal is quite high but the feedback taken for the redressal of Grievance is not at 
par with the pace of grievance redressal. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department to increase the number of seats in the Feedback call centre developed by 
the Department so that the number of feedbacks can be enhanced. The Committee also 
recommends the Department to develop a mechanism in which as soon as the Grievance 
is disposed a SMS stating the details of disposal is received on the Mobile of the 
complainant and where he/she can submit the feedback of the Grievance Redressal 
alongwith the option to appeal if he/she is not satisfied with the redressal of grievance. 
3.9 The Committee recommends identifying "Scheme-wise complaints" by using 
Data Strategy Unit (DSU) which is functioning under the Department. 
3.10 The Committee also recommends the Department to use Artificial Intelligence to 
develop a mechanism in which grievance can be lodged through voice recording which 
will help the people who are unable to file grievances using CPGRAMS portal. 

 29 
3.11 The Committee has observed that the percentage of grievances redressed over 
the past 5 years for States is less compared to the percentage of grievances redressed 
over the past 5 years of Central Government. The Committee, therefore, urges the 
Department to take it up with the State Governments to enhance their grievance 
disposal rate so that Public Grievances are addressed effectively. 
3.12 The Committee observes that DARPG in collaboration with National 
Informatics Centre (NIC) has developed 'My Grievance' mobile app for Android. The 
application is not compatible with the latest versions of Android and IOS software. The 
rating of the app is just 3.3 and also the reviews are very negative. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Department to make it compatible with the latest versions of 
Android and IOS software and also to find the shortcomings so that the application may 
improve its rating. 
e-Office - Mission Mode Project 
3.13 e-Office is one of the Mission Mode Projects (MMPs), under the National e-

3.14 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department in making e-Office

II. PENSION ADALATS 
3.48 This Department had started the unique experiment of holding Pension Adalats to 
resolve chronic grievances of Central Govt. Pensioners, falling within the four walls of extant 
policy. These Adalats, as the term might sound, do not have any judicial or quasi-judicial 
powers but have proved a highly successful mode of grievance resolution. All the stake-
holders of a particular grievance are invited on a single table viz. the concerned 
Ministry/Department, the Pay & Accounts Officer of the concerned Department, the CPAO 
(Central Pension Accounts Officer, Ministry of Finance), the concerned Bank and the 
Pensioner or his/her representative and they resolve the case across the table. 
3.49 The Departmental Parliamentary Standing Committee for Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances & Pensions in its 95th Report appreciated the system of holding Pension 
Adalats and suggested that a day may be dedicated to the Pensioners, as part of good 
governance, and efforts be made to minimize their grievances. The Committee suggested

this objective in view.

III. SANKALP 
3.53 A number of pensioners feel the loss of a daily routine as well as of feeling of not 
being wanted.  Keeping these factors in mind a new initiative of the Department, christened 
as Sankalp, has been taken up to prepare them for post-retirement life and channelize 
experiences and skill of retired Government servants towards meaningful interventions in 
Society.  

 38 
3.54 Under this initiative the Department is also conducting Pre-Retirement Counseling 
Sessions (PRCs) for employees retiring in near future. 48 PRCs have been conducted till date 
which benefited 6572 retiring/retired personnel of various Ministries and Departments of 
Government of India. PRC covers aspects relating to timely payment of pension and 
processing formalities, CGHS benefits available to pensioners, investment options, income 
tax incentives for senior citizens/pensioners, preparation of Will and post retirement 
voluntary effort. 
IV. ANUBHAV  
3.55 Anubhav is a platform for retiring government employees to share their experience of 
working with the Government.  It is envisaged that Anubhav will be nurtured as a tool for 
creating institutional memory. Till date 92 organizations have registered, 8924 write-ups have 
been published and 4729 write-ups which have been uploaded and are waiting to be 
published.  
3.56 An Annual Award Scheme to incentivize and encourage more retiring employees to 
submit their write-ups was introduced. Till date 4 award ceremonies have been organized in 
which 35 awardees was conferred appreciation for their Anubhav write-ups. 
V. PENSIONERS’ ASSOCIATIONS 
3.57 While initiating the Pensioners‟ Portal, it was envisaged to engage a large number of 
Pensioners‟ Associations in the successful implementation and continuing operation of the 
above mechanism, so as to make it largely self-sustaining. DoPPW has identified 50 
Pensioners‟ Associations from across the country and involved them for effective 
implementation of the Pensioners Portal.  These Associations help pensioners in filing their 
grievances online through CPENGRAMS, pursue the cases with the concerned authorities at 
various levels and also take up various activities for the welfare of pensioners besides 
increasing general awareness amongst retiring and retired Govt. servants about retirement and 
pension related matters.  
3.58 The Committee commends the overall performance of the Department of 
Pension and Pensioners Welfare and hopes that it will continue with its good work to 
bring about 'ease of living' for pensioners, especially for super senior citizens and family 
pensioners.

CHAPTER-I 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Minstry of Law & Justice 
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by 
the British Parliament. The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in 
administration of justice; furnishing legal advice to the Government of India and defending 
Government of India in various Courts and Tribunals; drafting Supreme and Subordinate 
legislations for Government of India; appointment, resignation and removal of Judges of the 
Supreme Court of India and High Courts in States; Legal aid to poor; access to Justice; 
Justice Delivery & Legal Reforms; etc. 
1.1 The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Legislative Department; 
(ii) Department of Legal Affairs; and 
(iii) Department of Justice. 
 
Chart No. 1.0 
 
1.2 The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Minister of Law and Justice 
assisted by a Minister of State. Each of the three departments is administratively headed by 
an independent Secretary. 
1.3 This report is on the Department of Justice.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
Functions of the Department 
 
1.4 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, functions of the 
Department are as under: 
i. Appointment, resignation and removal of the Chief Justice of India and Judges 
of the Supreme Court of India; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of 
absence (including leave allowance), pensions and travelling allowances; 
ii. Appointment, resignation and removal etc. of Chief Justice and Judges of 
High Courts in States; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence 
(including leave allowances), pensions and travelling allowances; 
iii. Appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial Officers in Union 
Territories; 
iv. Constitution and organization (excluding jurisdiction and powers) of the 
Supreme Court (but including contempt of such Court) and the fees taken 
therein; 
v. Constitution and organization of the High Courts and the Courts of Judicial 
Commissioners except provisions as to officers and servants of these courts; 
vi. Administration of justice and constitution and organization of courts in the 
Union Territories and fees taken in such courts; 
vii. Courts fees and Stamp duties in the Union Territories; 
viii. Creation of All India Judicial Service; 
ix. Conditions of service of District Judges and other Members of Higher Judicial 
Service of Union Territories; 
x. Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory or exclusion 
of a Union Territory from the Jurisdiction of a High Court; 
xi. Legal Aid to the poor; 
xii. Administration of Justice; and 
xiii. Access to Justice, Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms.

1.14 The primary responsibility for development of judicial infrastructure in the States 
rests with the State Governments.   The Central Government augments the resources of the 
State Governments by providing financial assistance under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
(CSS) for Development of I nfrastructure Facilities for Judiciary.   The Scheme is in force 
since 1993-94.  It covers the construction of court buildings and residential accommodations 
of judicial officers of District and Subordinate Judiciary.  However, the scheme does not 
cover construction of High Court buildings. 
 
1.15 Presently, the fund sharing pattern of the Scheme is 90:10 (centre: state) for the 8 
North-Eastern States and 2 Himalayan States (Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh) and 60:40 
for the rest of the States. There is 100% assistance for Union Territories. 
 
1.16 The scheme was evaluated by NITI Aayog and its continuance was recommended. 
Accordingly, the Government has approved the continuance of this CSS for a period of 5 
more years i.e. from 2021 -22 to 2025-26 with financial outlay of Rs. 9,000 crores (including 
central share of Rs. 5,307 crore). Now, in addition to the construction of Court Halls and 
Residential Units for Judges/Judicial Officer of D istrict and Subordinate Courts, the Scheme 
would now also cover construction of Lawyers‟ Hall, Toilet Complexes and Digital 
Computer Rooms.

1.18 The State is duty bound to provide easy access to Justice and timely delivery of 
Justice to all its citizen. Adequacy of judicial infrastructure plays a critical role in 
reduction of pendency and backlog of cases in the Courts. But it is an undeniable fact  
that the state of judicial infrastructure in the country is far from being satisfactory. 
Courts are functioning in rented premises with insufficient space and many in a 
dilapidated condition without basic amenities like toilets  etc. In such a scenario, the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for 
Judiciary is playing a pivotal role in the development of critical infrastructure at the 
State level. 
 
1.19 From the data provided by the Department of Justice it can be seen that many of 
the States are utilizing this scheme in the best possible manner and  have created  
substantial judicial infrastructure in their States. However, in many of the States 
nothing notable has happened under this Scheme.  
 
1.20 The Committee observes that t he pace of release of funds has slowed down due 
to revised procedural guidelines for release of CSS funds under the new Public 
Financial Management System (PFMS). Due to stringent conditions attached for release 
of funds, most of the States are  finding it difficult to get their quota of funds despite 
having huge requirements for funds for their projects both ongoing and new. From the 
data provided by the Department, 11 out of 21 general category States and 5 out of 8 
NE States did not get any fu nds during 2022 -23 due to such norms. Though the 
Committee is happy to note that the Department of Justice is taking all possible 
measures to ameliorate the hardship faced by the States in this regard, and to ensure 
that all of them become PFMS compliant , the Committee , however, recommends the 
Department to approach the MoF to get the guidelines on release of funds under the 
CSS relaxed, wherever the States are facing genuine difficulties in the implementation 
of such guidelines.  
 
1.21 The Committee in Jan uary, 2023 visited Assam, Manipur and Tripura to assess 
the judicial infrastructure and to have an on the spot assessment of implementation of 
this Scheme in the North East ern region. After deliberating with the concerned State 
Governments and High Court Judges on this issue the Committee is constrained to note 
that the status of judicial infrastructure is in very bad shape in the region and they are 
not being able to make full use of this Scheme. 
 
1.22 Apart from general PFMS related issues being faced by all the States/UTs, the 
North-Eastern States have their own issues because of their peculiar topography which 
makes availability of unencumbered land a bit difficult. Also the NE States and other 
hilly States are bestowed with short working season which makes movement of men and 
material difficult over the treacherous terrain and thereby making contract 
implementation difficult with increased time and cost overruns. Because of limited 
railways connectivi ty in the region, the cost of transportation becomes much higher, 

 19 
leading to substantial increase in cost of material. Other reasons include late receipt of 
project proposals and non -receipt of utilization of certificates from the respective state 
governments. It has also been found that in case of North -eastern States, their 
contribution to the scheme though meagre (only 10% vis -à-vis 90% of Central share) 
gets delayed. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department to explore the 
possibility of prov iding a better deal in terms of enhanced allocation of funds and 
relaxation of spending norms under the Scheme, considering the peculiarities of the NE 
States. It is further recommended that the 10% of the state quota may also be relaxed 
for the NE States subject to subsequent recovery from the concerned state , so that the 
ongoing projects are not stalled for want of such meagre amount of money.

(iii) eCourts Mission Mode Project 
 
1.30 As part of the National eGovernance Plan, the eCourts Project is an integrated 
Mission Mode Project under implementation since 2007 for ICT development of the Indian 
Judiciary based on the “National Policy and Action Plan for Implementation of Information 
and Communication Technology in the Indian Judiciary”. The e -Court Integrated Mission 
Mode Project was launched with the objective of improving access to justice using 
technology.  Against the financial outlay of Rs.1670.00 crore in Phase II of the Project, the 
Department of Justice has released Rs.1668.43 crore for implementation of the Project till 

 21 
31st March 2022.  Under Phase -II, 18,735 District & Subordinate Courts have been 
computerized so far. The entire allocation for eCourts Project Phase -II has been exhausted by 
31st March, 2022. 
 
1.31 The Detailed Project Report of the e -Courts Project Phase -III has been approved by 
eCommittee, Supreme Court of India on 21st October, 2022 under the chairmanship of 
Hon‟ble Dr. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud . The Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) Note for 
e-Courts Project Phase -III is under consideration with the Department of Expenditure, 
Ministry of Finance.  The Government has announced allocation of Rs.7000.00 crore for the 
eCourts Project Phase-III in the Budget 2023. 
 
1.32 eCourts Phase-III: A Detailed Project Report (DPR) for eCourts Phase -III has been 
finalised and approved by eCommittee on 21 st October 2022. The projected budget for Phase-
III is Rs. 7210.20 crores and the final approval of the project is yet to be obtained from the 
Union Cabinet. However, as stated above, in the Union Budget 2023 -24 Government has 
announced Rs. 7000 Cr. for eCourts phase III. 
 
1.33 The Department in their presentation before the Committee has informed that eCourts 
Phase-III essentially focuses on the following: 
 
(i) To bridge the digital divide, fully functional e -Sewa Kendras in all court 
complexes. 
(ii) Implementation of  paperless courts in phase -wise manner, with all commercial 
courts becoming paperless in the first instance. 
(iii) Digitisation of the entire court records, both legacy records and pending cases. 
(iv) Intends to take Indian Judiciary to next level by use of emerging technologies like 
Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning etc. for analysis of case pendency, 
forecasting future litigation which will provide the building blocks for time bound 
disposal of cases, door step judicial services and ease of justice to all. 
 
1.34 eCourts Mission Mode Project is an important Scheme of the Department aimed 
at improving access to justice using technology. The Government has released a total of 
Rs. 935 crores and Rs. 1670 crores under Phase I and Phase II of the Scheme, 
respectively. The Committee is appreciative of the fact that Phase -II of the project has 
performed exceedingly well. But the Committee in its visits to many of the High Courts 
in the country have found that after the waning of the pandemic many of the Judges are 
not comfortable working with  the virtual/hybrid courts and are back to old mode of 
physical hearings. Thus there is a real danger of infrastructure created under this 
project on the hard -earned public money being wasted.  Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends the Government to approach the eCommittee of the Supreme Court and to 
request them to issue guidelines for making full use of e -resources created for 
virtual/hybrid hearings in the courts, which is not only time saving but also economical.  
 

 22 
1.35 The phase II of the eCourts Mission Mode Project ended on 31.03.2022. There 
has been no allocation for the phase III since then and for 2023 -24 also there has been 
no allocation. The Committee has been apprised that though the phase III has been 
finalized by the e Committee of the Supreme Court, it has yet to receive the approval of 
the Union Cabinet. However, the Government has announced Rs. 7,000 crores for 
eCourts Phase III in the Union Budget 2023-24. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Department to get ne cessary approvals for Phase III on priority and approach the 
MoF for further allocation on priority.

1.36 Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice in India (DISHA) has 
been designed by consolidating the programmes of Tele -Law, Pro Bono Legal Services, 
Nyaya Mitra and Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness programmes in the North Eastern 
States and UTs of J&K and Ladakh and upscaling these programmes to National level. The 
scheme aims to provide a multi-stakeholder, progressive and transformative approach with an 
integrated IEC and technology component. 
 
1.37 DISHA with a Pan India outlook serves as an omnibus and unified approach in 
strengthening access to justice for the socially disadvantaged, legally vulnerable groups and 
those categories of citizens identified who are for legal aid under Section 12 of Legal 
Services Authorities Act, 198 7. The details of various components of the Scheme are as 
under: 
 
Tele-Law: Tele-Law is an effective and reliable e - interface platform which aims 
to empower people by providing pre -litigation advice. It connects people, especially 
needy and disadvantaged sections, to Panel Lawyers via video conference/telephone 
facilities available at Common Service Centres (CSCs) across the country. 
 
Nyaya- Bandhu (Pro-Bono Legal Services): This programme is the 
Department‟s initiative to spearhead Pro -bono lawyering culture across the country. 
To further the initiative, Nyaya Bandhu Apps (Android & iOS) applications have 
been developed and also on boarded on UMANG platform to create a database of 
pro bono advocates. Mobile App is available in 6 languages – English, Hindi, Tamil, 
Telugu, Marathi and Punjabi. 5817 Advocates have registered under the programme 
till 31st January 2023. Further, Pro Bono Club Scheme has been rolled out to instill 
in the young minds an understanding and philosophy on Pro bono and to assist t he 
registered Pro Bono advocates in researching and legal drafting. 69 Law Schools 

 23 
across India have implemented the Pro Bono Club Scheme. Under MoU singed 
between Department of Justice and NALSA, District Legal Services Authority 
advocates to be empanelle d as Pro Bono advocates creating DLSA Panel under 
Nyaya Bandhu Programme. 
 
Nyaya Mitra: Nyaya Mitra aims to facilitate expeditious disposal of decade 
old pending cases in High Courts and Subordinate Courts. Since April 2017, a total 
number of 28 Nyaya Mitras were engaged in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West 
Bengal, Rajasthan, Odisha, Maharashtra and Tripura who assisted the courts 
concerned in disposal of old cases.  Nyaya Mitras who were engaged have helped in 
disposal of 2019 old cases, which includ e civil cases such as matrimonial cases, 
accident claim cases and also criminal cases. No fresh Nyaya Mitra could be 
engaged during the year 2020 -2021 due to closure of courts and social distancing 
protocols caused by Covid pandemic. In the year 2021 -22, 1 1 Nyaya Mitras are 
placed at 11 District Courts in the states of Assam, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, 
Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal & helped in disposal of 6000+ cases pending from 15 
years. 
 
Pan India Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Programme: Department of 
Justice, through its “Access to Justice NEJK Project”, undertook the local 
initiatives to address the legal needs of the marginalized and vulnerable sections of 
the society,  to improve the capacity of  justice delivery systems and legal services 
authority and to enhance legal awareness of the vulnerable populations in the 
States/UTs. Focus areas include Legal Aid, Legal Awareness and Legal Literacy. 
From 2012 to 2021 under the Access to Justice NEJK Project reached out to 
4,81,233 beneficiaries, conduct ed 4390 Legal Awareness/ Legal Literacy 
programmes, disseminated 8,30,900 copies of simplified IEC materials on 69 laws in 
26 languages/ dialects, trained and sensitized 20,672 Master Trainers including 6000 
students and 1884 Village Chiefs and established  158 community level Legal Aid 
Clinics. Under the DISHA Scheme, this initiative is now expanded as Pan -India 
Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Programme. In partnership with 13 
implementing organizations and through series of capacity building programmes and 
community level Legal Awareness Programmes, Pan-India Legal Literacy and Legal 
Awareness Programme reached out to 1,49,870 beneficiaries till December 2022.  
 
1.38 The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Department under the DISHA 
Scheme which  seeks to prioritize citizen -centric justice delivery system by integrating 
access to justice with technology. The four components of the Scheme has been curated 
with the objective of strengthening pre -litigation mechanism (Tele -Law); developing 
effective dispensation of pro-bono legal services (Nyaya Bandhu); facilitating disposal of 
pending cases in the courts through a cadre of retired Judges (Nyaya Mitra); and 
empowering citizens through pan-India legal literacy and legal awareness.  
 

 24 
1.39 In this connection the Committee would like to advise the Department that apart 
from their ongoing efforts, they should make full use of social media platforms like 
YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, etc. through supply of quality content on legal literacy 
and legal awareness  to the citizens . These platforms have a wider reach , even to the 
grassroots and are affordable to the citizens. The Department may use animations, talks 
by experts, etc. by way of making short videos , for educating the common public on 
their rights and also to generate awareness about the schemes/programmes of the 
Department.

VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
1.45 The Department of Justice was carved out as an independent Department from the 
Ministry of Home Affairs on 1st January, 2010.  However, the staff posted to the Department 
of Justice is borne on the common cadre with the M/o Home Affairs.  All staff related matters 
including recruitment of vacant posts to the common cadre is carried out by the M/o Home 
Affairs and staff posted to the Department of Justice.  Due to non - filling of vacant posts by 
the M/o Home Affairs, vacant posts could not be filled up in the Department.  The 
Department of Justice has informed that they are continuously reminding M/o Home Affairs  
and DoPT (which is the cadre controlling authority of majority of posts) from time to time to 
fill up the vacant posts but all in vain. 
 
1.46 The Department has informed that to cope up with the extreme shortage of staff, 
besides requesting M/o Home Affai rs and DoPT to fill the vacancies, Department has 
engaged retired Government servants as consultants and also hired outsourced staff i.e. Data 
Entry Operators and Multi Tasking Staff. This Department has also apprised that they have 
also been requesting Do PT to allot staff of Central Secretariat Cadre directly to the 
Department of Justice; however, nothing has happened in this regard.

1.55 Hon‟ble Supreme Court while hearing WP(C) 13 of 2015 in NJAC matter issued 
detailed Order on 16 -12-2015 on supplementing the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) and 
laid down that Government of India may finalize the Memorandum of Procedure by 
supplementing it in consultation with the Chief Justic e of India.  The Chief Justice of India 
will take a decision based on the unanimous view of the Collegium comprising of four 
senior-most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court. The order stated that they shall take the 
following factors into consideration such  as eligibility criterion, transparency in the 
appointment process, secretariat, complaint mechanism and miscellaneous matter considered 
appropriate for ensuring transparency and accountability including interaction with the 
recommendees by the Collegium of the Supreme Court without sacrificing the confidentiality 
of appointment. 
 
1.56 In pursuance of the above orders, the Government of India sent the revised MoP to 
Hon'ble Chief Justice of India on 22.3.2016, the response of the Supreme Court Collegium on 
the revised draft MoP was received on 25.05.2016 and 01.07.2016. The view of the 
Government in response to the views of the SCC was conveyed to the CJI on 03.08.2016. 

 29 
The view of the Government in response to the views of the Supreme Court Collegium was 
conveyed to the CJI on 03.08.2016. Comments of SCC on the views of Government on the 
draft MoP received on 13.03.2017. 
 
1.57 The Government has informed the Committee that in view of various judicial 
pronouncements and suggestions by the Supreme Court, the G overnment in its recent 
communication dated 06.01.2023 to the Chief Justice of India, has emphasized on the need to 
finalize the MoP.  The Government is yet to receive a response on this issue from the 
Supreme Court. 
 
1.58 The Committee observes that the S upreme Court and the Government have 
failed to reach a consensus on revision of the Memorandum of Procedure (MOP) for 
appointment of Judges to the constitutional courts, though the same is under 
consideration of both for about seven years now. The Committe e expects the 
Government and the Judiciary to weed out their differences and to finalize the revised 
MOP, which is more efficient and transparent, in terms of the Supreme Court 
observation cited above.

CHAPTER-II 
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY 
 
2.0 Article 39A of the Constitution of India provides for free legal aid to the poor and 
weaker sections of the society and ensures justice for all. Also, Articles 14 and 22 (1) of the 
Constitution also make it obligatory for the State to ensure equality b efore law and a legal 
system which promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity to all. In this background, 
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted by the Parliament, which came into 
force on 9 th November, 1995 to establish a nationwide network for providing free and 
competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society on the basis of equal 
opportunity. 
 
2.1 The NALSA monitors and evaluates implementation of legal aid programmes and 
lays down policies and principles for making l egal services available under the Act. In every 
State, a State Legal Services Authority and in every High Court, a High Court Legal Services 
Committee has been constituted. District Legal Services Authorities, Taluk Legal Services 
Committees have been cons tituted in the Districts and most of the Taluks, respectively, to 
give effect to the policies and directions of the NALSA and to provide free legal services to 
the people and conduct Lok Adalats in the State. Supreme Court Legal Services Committee 
has been constituted to administer and implement the legal services programme insofar as it 
relates to the Supreme Court of India. 
 
FUNCTIONS OF NALSA 
 
2.2 The details of activities/programmes regarding Legal Aid and Advice undertaken by 
Legal Services Authorities  under the aegis of National Legal Services Authority are as 
follows:  
  
(i)       Legal aid and advice: Free Legal aid and assistance in the form of 
representation, drafting of notices, replies and legal advice is being provided by Legal 
Services Institutions at all levels free of cost to the eligible persons. The legal assistance 
is also provided to legal aid seekers by assigning panel lawyers to them for 
representation before the courts and for drafting petitions and notices. 
  
(ii)    Legal Services at Pre-Arrest, Arrest and Remand Stage: NALSA prepared 
a protocol in 2019 for providing access to justice to suspects and arrestees. The protocol 
spells out a framework for providing legal assistance at pre -arrest, arrest and remand 
stages. The protocol is expected to fulfill the following objectives: 
 
 To provide legal assistance to needy suspects and arrestees during 
interrogation and other early stages of investigation. 
 To decrease the vulnerabilities of suspects and arrestees. 
 To assist in avoiding unnecessary arrests 

 31 
 To assist the arrestees in filing bail applications and furnishing bail bonds.   
 
 (iii)  Legal Aid Defense Counsel System (LADCS): To provide competent, 
effective and efficient legal aid and to make legal services more professional, NALSA 
has developed a legal aid delivery-based model i.e. „Legal Aid Defense Counsel System‟ 
(LADCS) for proving legal aid in criminal matters on the lines of public defender system 
in the developed countries. LADCS has been introduced to provide representation in all 
type of criminal matters through engagement of full -time retainer lawyers, exclusively 
dealing with legal aid criminal cases in 676 Districts  across the country. Presently, a 
Legal Aid seeker is assigned a lawyer from the panel of lawyers maintained in the 
district.  These panel lawyers also have private practice and often it has come to light 
that they are unable to devote sufficient time to the legal aid cases.  Therefore, Legal Aid 
Defence Counsel System aims to set up office of Defence Counsel System just like 
office of prosecution in line of public defender system prevailing in developed countries. 
The Lawyers appointed under the Defence Counsel System will devote entire time to the 
criminal legal aid cases assigned to them on retainership basis on monthly salary and 
they are prohibited from taking up any private practice. This will directly result in 
increasing the quality and efficiency in service provided to the legal aid beneficiary. 
 
(iv)  Front Office: Front Offices/ Consultation Offices are manned by the panel 
lawyers and one or more PLVs available during office hours. In the case of court based 
legal services, such lawyers shall after consideration of the application, forward the same 
to the Committee set up under regulations 7 and for other types of legal services, the 
panel lawyers in the front offices may provide such legal services. The panel lawyers in 
the front office shall rende r service like drafting notice, sending replies to lawyers, 
noting and drafting applications, petitions etc.   
 
(v)  Web portal: NALSA has created a web portal to file Applications through 
online for getting legal assistance.  The applicant may file the ap plications either directly 
to State Legal Services Authority/District Legal Services Authority/High Court Legal 
Services Committee/Supreme Court Legal Services Committee from where the applicant 
requires legal assistance.  The applicant has the option to f ile application directly to 
NALSA and in that case the said application is transferred to the concerned Legal 
Services Institutions for appropriate action i.e. to provide legal assistance.  Thereafter, 
the concerned Legal Services Institution has to update the action taken report. The online 
web portal for filing legal aid applications has also been made more inclusive and a legal 
aid application can now be filed in Ten (10) languages i.e. English, Hindi, Marathi, 
Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, Gujarati, Bengali, Odia and Kannada. 
 
(vi)  Mobile App: NALSA has launched Legal Services Mobile App for Android 
and IOS version. It will facilitate following functions: 
 
 Any citizen may apply for seeking legal assistance, legal advice and for 
redressal of other grievances through Mobile App.  

 32 
 Any citizen may track his application submitted for legal aid & advice 
and other grievances.  
 Reminder can be sent and clarifications can be sought through Mobile 
App. 
 Any victim of crime or applicant can apply for victim compensation  
through the Mobile App.  
 Application for pre -institution mediation in commercial matters or 
application for mediation may be filed through this Mobile App. 
 Besides above, Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs), Helpline assistance 
and assistance through e-mail are also provided in the Mobile App.    
 
(vii)   Tele-Law: Under the programme the services of panel lawyers of Legal 
Services Authorities will be availed to provide legal advice and consultation through the 
use of tele/ video conferencing facilities avai lable at the Common Services Centres or 
directly through the citizens tele law mobile application and in person at front offices of 
District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) and State Legal Services Authorities 
(SLSAs). 
 
2.3 As informed by NALSA the Legal Aid Defence Counsel Scheme (LADCS) 
engages full-time experienced lawyers to exclusively devote their effort to provide legal 
aid, assistance and representation to the beneficiaries in criminal matters. This is a 
paradigm shift in the manner in which the legal aid is provided in the country, whereas 
earlier cases were assigned to the empanelled lawyers who also had a private practice. 
The Committee appreciates such scheme and hope that it will improve the quality of 
legal aid to the beneficiary. It is also expected that competent and dedicated lawyers are 
empanelled through a transparent selection process for manning this Scheme.

2.7 The Committee in its 116 th Report while referring to the fact that per capita free 
legal aid spending in India is perhaps the lowest in the World and had recommended a 
substantial increase in the Grant -in-aid given to NALSA. It is a harsh reality that the 
prevalent social and econo mic disparity in the country is eroding the democratic

Council. The Academy is fully funded by the Government of India.

education; 
 Coordinate and monitor the functioning of NJA & SJAs; and 
 Suggest methods for improving judicial education facilities and cooperation among

CHAPTER – IV 
SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
4.0 The Supreme Court of India is at the apex of a pyramidal, unified and integrated 
judicial system. Though the political system of the country is federal in nature, the judicial 
system is unitary. The Supreme Court came into existence on 28th January, 1950 and as of 
now it comprises the Chief Justice of India and 33 Judges. The strength of the apex court was 
enhanced over the years from 8 in 1950 to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986, 31 
in 2009 and 34 in 2019, with the increase of case load on it. The Constitution of India 
provides for the Supreme Court to be a court of record, guardian of liberties & rights and also 
as the final arbiter in most disputes. It is an appellate court, can review its own judgement and 
in its advisory capacity may answer references by the President on any question of law of 
public importance. The Supreme Court is designated as the custodian of fundamental rights 
and the 'rule of law'. It has power of judicial review and the law declared by the Supreme 
Court is binding on all courts. 
4.1 The administrative wing of the Supreme Court is called 'Registry'. The Registry is 
divided into two wings - (i) Administrative Wing; and (ii) Judicial Wing. These wings are 
further divided into various Divisions, Branches, Sections and Cells. The Chief Justice of 
India is the Administrative head of the Supreme Court. The highest Administrative Officer of 
the Supreme Court is the Secretary General, the post manned by a judicial officer of the rank 
of a District & Sessions Judge and is of the rank of Secretary to the Government of India. The 
Secretary General is assisted by Registrars, Officers on Special Duty, Additional Registrars, 
Deputy Registrars, officers of other lower ranks and subordinate staff. 
4.2 The Department of Justice is the nodal Department for the Supreme Court of India. 
There is a separate demand, Demand No. 67 pertaining to the Supreme Court of India, which 
is entirely charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India and cannot be submitted to the vote 
of Parliament. However, Article 113 of the Constitution provides for those estimates to be 
discussed in either House of Parliament.

Observations/Recommendations at a Glance 
 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for 
Judiciary 
 
1. The State is duty bound to provide easy access to Justice and timely delivery 
of Justice to all its  citizen. Adequacy of judicial infrastructure plays a critical 
role in reduction of pendency and backlog of cases in the Courts. But it is an 
undeniable fact that the state of judicial infrastructure in the country is far 
from being satisfactory. Courts ar e functioning in rented premises with 
insufficient space and many in a dilapidated condition without basic amenities 
like toilets etc. In such a scenario, the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for 
Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judiciary is playing a pivotal role 
in the development of critical infrastructure at the State level. (1.18) 
 
2. From the data provided by the Department of Justice it can be seen that many 
of the States are utilizing this scheme in the best possible manner and have 
created substantial judicial infrastructure in their States. However, in many 
of the States nothing notable has happened under this Scheme. (1.19) 
 
3. The Committee observes that the pace of release of funds has slowed down 
due to revised procedural guidelines for r elease of CSS funds under the new 
Public Financial Management System (PFMS). Due to stringent conditions 
attached for release of funds, most of the States are finding it difficult to get 
their quota of funds despite having huge requirements for funds for t heir 
projects both ongoing and new. From the data provided by the Department, 
11 out of 21 general category States and 5 out of 8 NE States did not get any 
funds during 2022 -23 due to such norms. Though the Committee is happy to 
note that the Department of  Justice is taking all possible measures to 
ameliorate the hardship faced by the States in this regard, and to ensure that 
all of them become PFMS compliant, the Committee, however, recommends 
the Department to approach the MoF to get the guidelines on rel ease of funds 
under the CSS relaxed wherever the States are facing genuine difficulties in 
the implementation of such guidelines. (1.20) 
 
4. The Committee in January, 2023 visited Assam, Manipur and Tripura to 
assess the judicial infrastructure and to have an  on the spot assessment of 
implementation of this Scheme in the North Eastern region. After deliberating 
with the concerned State Governments and High Court Judges on this issue 

 43 
the Committee is constrained to note that the status of judicial infrastructur e 
is in very bad shape in the region and they are not being able to make full use 
of this Scheme. (1.21) 
 
5. Apart from general PFMS related issues being faced by all the States/UTs, the 
North-Eastern States have their own issues because of their peculiar 
topography which makes availability of unencumbered land a bit difficult. 
Also the NE States and other hilly States are bestowed with short working 
season which makes movement of men and material difficult over the 
treacherous terrain and thereby making contr act implementation difficult 
with increased time and cost overruns. Because of limited railways 
connectivity in the region, the cost of transportation becomes much higher, 
leading to substantial increase in cost of material. Other reasons include late 
receipt of project proposals and non -receipt of utilization of certificates from 
the respective state governments. It has also been found that in case of North -
eastern States, their contribution to the scheme though meagre (only 10% vis -
à-vis 90% of Central sh are) gets delayed. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends the Department to explore the possibility of providing a better 
deal in terms of enhanced allocation of funds and relaxation of spending 
norms under the Scheme, considering the peculiarities of the N E States. It is 
further recommended that the 10% of the state quota may also be relaxed for 
the NE States subject to subsequent recovery from the concerned state, so that 
the ongoing projects are not stalled for want of such meagre amount of 
money. (1.22) 
 
Assistance to State Governments for establishing and operationalising Gram 
Nyayalayas 
 
6. Assistance to State Governments for establishing and operationalising Gram 
Nyayalayas is a small Scheme with a financial outlay of Rs. 50 cores from 
2021-22 to 2025 -26. Further, the concept of Gram Nyayalayas has failed to 
take off in most of the States which are not keen to operationalise it due to 
their local problems. Only 264 Gram Nyayalayas are functional out of 476 
notified. Though, there are instances where some s tates have operationalized 
their Gram Nyayalayas without any central assistance. (1.28) 
 
7. In view of the above, the Committee recommends the Government to evaluate 
the utility continuing such a Scheme and to divert the funds earmarked for 
this Scheme to the  CSS for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for 
Judiciary. (1.29) 
 
 
 
 

 44 
eCourts Mission Mode Project 
 
8. eCourts Mission Mode Project is an important Scheme of the Department 
aimed at improving access to justice using technology. The Government has 
released a total of Rs. 935 crores and Rs. 1670 crores under Phase I and Phase 
II of the Scheme, respectively. The Comm ittee is appreciative of the fact that 
Phase-II of the project has performed exceedingly well. But the Committee in 
its visits to many of the High Courts in the country have found that after the 
waning of the pandemic many of the Judges are not comfortable working with 
the virtual/hybrid courts and are back to old mode of physical hearings. Thus 
there is a real danger of infrastructure created under this project on the hard-
earned public money being wasted.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends 
the Governm ent to approach the eCommittee of the Supreme Court and to 
request them to issue guidelines for making full use of e -resources created for 
virtual/hybrid hearings in the courts, which is not only time saving but also 
economical. (1.34) 
 
9. The phase II of the eCourts Mission Mode Project ended on 31.03.2022. There 
has been no allocation for the phase III since then and for 2023 -24 also there 
has been no allocation. The Committee has been apprised that though the 
phase III has been finalized by the eCommittee o f the Supreme Court, it has 
yet to receive the approval of the Union Cabinet. However, the Government 
has announced Rs. 7,000 crores for eCourts Phase III in the Union Budget 
2023-24. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to get 
necessary app rovals for Phase III on priority and approach the MoF for 
further allocation on priority. (1.35) 
 
Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice in India (DISHA) 
 
10. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Department under the 
DISHA Scheme which seeks to prioritize citizen -centric justice delivery 
system by integrating access to justice with technology. The four components 
of the Scheme has been curated with t he objective of strengthening pre -
litigation mechanism (Tele -Law); developing effective dispensation of pro -
bono legal services (Nyaya Bandhu); facilitating disposal of pending cases in 
the courts through a cadre of retired Judges (Nyaya Mitra); and empowe ring 
citizens through pan-India legal literacy and legal awareness. (1.38) 
 
11. In this connection the Committee would like to advise the Department that 
apart from their ongoing efforts, they should make full use of social media 
platforms like YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, etc. through supply of quality 
content on legal literacy and legal awareness to the citizens. These platforms 
have a wider reach, even to the grassroots and are affordable to the citizens. 
The Department may use animations, talks by expe rts, etc. by way of making 

 45 
short videos, for educating the common public on their rights and also to 
generate awareness about the schemes/programmes of the Department. (1.39) 
 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for setting up of Fast Track Special Courts (FTSC) 
for trail of cases related to rape and POCSO Act 
 
12. As per the data provided by the Department, the Committee observes that the 
pace of registration of rape and POCSO Act cas es is much more than their 
disposal rate.  Resultantly, as on 31.12.2022, more than 3.5 lakh cases of rape 
and POCSO Act are still pending across the country in various courts. 
Further, being a CSS scheme, State's contribution is also required in 
prescribed share; further, the consent of State Governments is also required 
for setting up of FTSCs in the States. Despite repeated requests, interventions 
at various levels, the Department is still awaiting consent from the State 
Government of West Bengal, which has been allocated 123 FTSCs. Also, some 
other States have not operationalized all the FTSCs allocated to them. Besides 
this one of the major reasons being non -availability of Judicial Officers to 
man these FTSCs. (1.43) 
 
13. In view of the above factors which  are plaguing the Scheme, the Committee, 
recommends that in addition to establishment of more FTSCs the Department 
should also study and suggest how systemic improvement may be brought 
about to overhaul the entire system of FTSCs. The Committee further 
recommends the Department to explore the best practices in other countries 
where FTCs are functional and have been able to dispose of cases in a time 
bound manner and to bring about the required changes in our system to make 
it more efficient. (1.44) 
 
VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
14. The Department even after 12 years of its separation from the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and becoming independent, is still dependent on the MHA for 
all its man power requirements. From the above table it can be seen that the  
vacancies in the Department is staggering. Accordingly, in the last DFG 
Report, the Committee had recommended that the Department of Justice 
should be given full autonomy in case of personnel management and all cadre 
controlling authorities, including DoPT, were asked to post all encadred posts 
directly to the Department of Justice. However, even after a year of the said 
recommendation the DoPT and MHA are yet to furnish their reply on the 
issue. (1.49) 
 
15. The Department of Justice is one of the better perfo rming Departments. The 
Department in their submission has informed that they are facing huge 
difficulties in the smooth functioning of the Department due to acute staff 

 46 
shortage. Accordingly, the Committee reiterates the above recommendation 
that the Depar tment should take up this matter with the highest level and 
action taken replies may be furnished to this Committee within three months 
time. (1.50) 
 
VACANCY OF JUDGES IN HIGHER JUDICIARY 
 
16. From the above table it can be seen that as on 31.12.2022, vacancies in the 
High Courts stands at 30% of the total strength. Six High Courts have 
vacancies of 40% and above and another six have vacancies in the range of 30 
% to 40%. Though the situation ha s improved over the last year, the 
vacancies at the High Court level are quite significant. (1.52) 
 
17. In Gujarat and Rajasthan the High Court is functioning with its half strength. 
In smaller states like Manipur, Tripura etc. where the bench strength is small, 
high levels of vacancies leads divisional benches not being constituted for want 
of judges and if there is some retirement or elevation or transfers the working 
of such High Courts are brought to a standstill. In the High Court of Tripura, 
where the Com mittee visited in the month of January, 2023, out of the 
sanctioned strength of 5, only 2 Judges were in -position, including the acting 
Chief Justice, making it difficult for them to constitute a divisional bench. 
Thus, these peculiarities of the smaller H igh Courts should be kept in mind 
while making appointments. (1.53) 
 
18. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department of Justice to fix all 
the bottlenecks responsible for delays in the appointment of Judges at the 
High Court. Only recently appointment s in the Supreme Court were done on 
a fast pace and it is functioning with full strength now. The appointments to 
High Courts also deserve same treatment and the vacancies must be filled 
with same zeal. (1.54) 
 
FINALIZATION OF MEMORANDA OF PROCEDURE (MOP) FOR 
APPOINTMENT OF SC/HC JUDGES 
 
19. The Committee observes that the Supreme Court and the Government have 
failed to reach a consensus on revision of the Memorandum of Procedure 
(MOP) for appointment of Judges to the constitutional courts, though the 
same is under consideration of both for about seven years now. The 
Committee expects the Government and the Judiciary to weed out their 
differences and to finalize the revised MOP, which is more efficient and 
transparent, in terms of the Supreme Court observation cited above. (1.58) 
 
 
 

 47 
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY 
 
20. As informed by NALSA the Legal Aid Defence Counsel Scheme (LADCS) 
engages full -time experienced lawyers to exclusively devote their effort to 
provide legal aid, assistance and representation to the beneficiaries in 
criminal matters. This is a paradigm shift in the manner in which the legal aid 
is provided in the country, whereas earlier cases were assigned to the 
empanelled lawyers who also had a private practice. The Committee 
appreciates such scheme and hope that it will improve the quality of legal aid 
to the beneficiary. It is also expected that competent and dedicated lawyers 
are empanelled through a transparent selection process for manning this 
Scheme. (2.3) 
 
ASSESSMENT OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
21. The Committee in its 116th Report while referring to the fact that per capita 
free legal aid spending in India is perhaps the lowest in the World and had 
recommended a substantial increase in the Grant-in-aid given to NALSA. It is 
a harsh reality that the prevalent social and economic disparity in the country 
is eroding the democratic objective of 'justice for all'. As majority of our 
population lack legal awareness and necessary means to approach the courts, 
they are compelled to suffer in silence. Legal aid is not a charity but an 
obligation of the State and right of the Citizen, it should be provided in the 
true spirit envisaged in the Constitution. (2.7) 
 
22. Thus there is an urgent need to give a major impetus to strengthen the legal 
aid movement in India by empowering the institutions like NALSA. 
Accordingly, the Committee strongly reiterates its recommendation that 
Grant-in-aid to NALSA should be substantial ly increased and for BE 2023 -24 
they should be provided with the amount projected by them to the MoF i.e. 
Rs. 400 crores, in order to carry out activities planned by them for the year 
2023-24. Without adequate budgetary provisions the ongoing and newly 
implemented schemes/activities of NALSA would fail to take off. The 
Department of Justice and NALSA should approach the MoF again and 
pursue the matter vigorously. (2.8) 
 
MANPOWER REQUIREMENT AT NALSA 
 
23. The Committee notes that NALSA's activities have increased manifold since 
its inception and it is actively engaged in taking the legal aid movement in 
India to every nook and corner. However, its existing sanctioned staff strength 
of 34 only is too low con sidering its mandate and reach. Accordingly, the 

 48 
Committee recommends the Government to sanction additional 40 posts as 
requested by them. (2.11) 
 
24. The Committee further recommends the NALSA to take proactive steps to fill 
up the vacant posts, in accordance  with their respective RRs, on regular basis 
and not to allow piling up of unfilled vacancies. (2.12) 
 
NATIONAL JUDICIAL ACADEMY, BHOPAL 
 
25. The mandate of the National Judicial Academy is strengthening the 
administration of Justice through Judicial Education, Research and Policy 
Development. Considering its mandate and infrastructure at its disposal, the 
Committee is of the view that the potential of the institution has remained 
underutilized over the years. There is a need to significantly enhance i ts 
performance to make it an institution of eminence. (3.6) 
 
26. The Committee notes that the Academy trains only Judges and officers of the 
Supreme Court. It is felt that the resources of the Academy may also be used 
for the betterment of other stakeholders l ike Lawyers. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends the Academy to consider training the Lawyers also, 
for which they may charge appropriate fees. (3.7) 
 
27. The Committee also notes that the academic positions in the Academy are 
very few and as on date only 17 academic positions are filled. Accordingly, 
there is a need to fillup the vacant posts on priority and asses the need for 
enhancement of academic position. It is further suggested that the NJA should 
consider inviting noted academicians from abroad as resource persons to 
further enrich the academic content offered by them. (3.8) 
 
SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
 
28. The SCI has been allocated Rs. 437.15 crores for BE 2023-24. The Registry 
has informed that the variation in BE 2023 -24 over RE 2022 -23 (7.81%) is 
mainly due to allocation of Rs. 35 Cr in BE 2023 -24 under the head IT (now

expenditure trend of the SCI has remained quite efficient as they have been 
able to timely utilize the funds allocated to them over the years. The 
Committee however expects the Government to allot the SCI the funds 
requirement projected by them, so that the activities initiated by them are 
completed on time. (4.4)

CHAPTER – I 
 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Ministry of Law & Justice 
1.0 The Ministry of Law & Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by the 
British Parliament. The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in 
administration of justice; furnishing legal advice to the Government of India and defending 
Government of India in various Courts and Tribunals; drafting Supreme and Subordinate 
legislations for Government of India; appointment, resignation and removal of Judges of the 
Supreme Court of India and High Courts in States; Legal aid to poor; access to Justice; 
Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms etc. 
1.1 The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Legislative Department; 
(ii) Department of Legal Affairs; and 
(iii) Department of Justice. 
 
1.2 The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Minister of Law and Justice 
assisted by a Minister of State. Each of the three departments is administratively headed by 
an independent Secretary. 
1.3 This report is on the Department of Legal Affairs.

DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
Functions of the Department 
1.4 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department 
of Legal Affairs has been allocated the following matters:  
(i) Advice to Ministries on legal matters including interpretation of the Constitution 
and the Laws, conveyancing an d engagement of counsel to appear on behalf of the 
Union of India in the High Courts and subordinate Courts, where the Union of 
India is a party. 
(ii) Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India, and other Central 
Government Law Officers of the States , whose services are shared by the 
Ministries of the Government of India. 
(iii) Conduct of cases in the Supreme Court of India and the High Courts on behalf of 
the Central Government and on behalf of the Governments of States participating 
in the Central Agency Scheme. 
(iv) Reciprocal arrangements with foreign countries for the service of summons in civil 
suits for the execution of decrees of Civil Courts, for the enforcement of 
maintenance orders, and for the administration of the estates of foreigners dying in 
India intestate. 
(v) Authorization of officers to execute contracts and assurances and of property on 
behalf of the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution, and authorization 
of officers to sign and verify plaints or written statements in suits by or ag ainst the 
Central Government. 
(vi) Indian Legal Service. 
(vii) Treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of civil law. 
(viii) Law Commission of India. 
(ix) Legal Profession including the Advocates Act, 1961 (25 of 1961) and persons 
entitled to practice before High Courts. 
(x) Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India and the conferring 
thereon of further powers; persons entitled to practise before the Supreme Court, 
references to the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution of India. 
(xi) Administration of the Notaries Act, 1952 (53 of 1952). 
(xii) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. 
1.5 Besides, the Department has also been allocated administration of the following acts: 
(a) The Advocates Act, 1961 
(b) The Notaries Act, 1952 
(c) The Advocates‟ Welfare Fund Act, 2001 
(d) The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 
(e) The India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019 

 11 
1.6 Additionally, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) and the Law Commission of 
India fall under the administrative purview of the Department. The Department is the cadre 
controlling authority of the Indian Legal Service (ILS). The Department also handles the 
appointment of the Attorney General of India, the Solicitor General of India, and the 
Additional Solicitor General of India. The Department also approves grant-in-aid to specific 
institutions like Indian Law Institute, for encouraging legal education and research and for the 
advancement of the legal profession.  
Structure of the Department 
1.7 The Main Secretariat of the Department of Legal Affairs is located in New Delhi, and 
Branch Secretariats are located at Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. The nature of 
duties discharged by the Department is broadly classified into two areas - Advice work and 
Litigation work. The Main Secretariat is headed by the Law Secretary, assisted by Additional 
Secretaries, Joint Secretary and several levels of Legal Advisers.  
1.8 There is a Central Agency Section in the Department, which is currently led by the 
Law Secretary and supported by Officers from the Government Advocates cadre of the ILS 
and other supporting staff, handles litigation at the Supreme Court on beh alf of all 
Ministries/Department of the Government of India as well as some administration of the 
Union Territories. The litigation work in High Courts and CAT (Principal Bench) is handled 
by the Litigation (High Court) Section and in Lower Courts by the L itigation (Lower Court) 
Section. 
1.9 The Department has a separate cell called the 'Implementation Cell' to handle the 
implementation of the recommendations of the Law commission of India and the 
administration of the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Advocates Welfare Fund Act, 2001. This 
Cell also administers the subject of 'Legal Education' as provided under Entry 26 of List III to 
the 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India.  
1.10 The Department tenders legal advice to all Ministries and Departments of the 
Government of India. The legal advice team of the Department is generally headed by an 
Additional Secretary or a Joint Secretary & Legal Adviser, who, in turn, is assisted by other 
officers at different levels. 
1.11 Under the Digital India initiative, the Department has created a web based application 
namely, Legal Information Management &  Briefing System (LIMBS) for monitoring all 
court cases where Union of India is a party. It is an innovative and easy to access online tool 
which is available 24x7 to all the stakeholders, viz., senior Government Officials, Nodal 
Officers and users of Mini stries/Department. LIMBS version 2.0 is an upgraded version of 
LIMBS and was launched in the year 2020 in collaboration with NIC.  
1.12 Further, the following Institutions/organizations are under the overall supervision of 
the Department of Legal Affairs: 

 12 
(i) Law Commission of India (LCI): - The Law Commission of India is a non-
statutory body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The 22nd Law 
Commission was constituted on 21.02.2020 for three years and is headed by Justice 
Ritu Raj Awasthi, Retired Chief Justice, Karnataka High Court along with three Full-
time Members and two Part-Time Members. The Commission is assisted by Law 
Officers of Indian Legal Service and a few consultants having experiences in legal 
research. A small group of secretarial staff looks after the administration. The Law 
Commission works on projects based on (a) Reference received from the Central 
Government and/or from Supreme Court of India and High Courts; and (b) Suo motu 
Cognizance - keeping in view the importance of the subject matter, the Commission 
may initiate study on specific subjects.  
(ii) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): - ITAT is one of the oldest Tribunals, 
set up under Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to hear second appeals in all 
matters of direct taxes and appeals against the revision orders of Administrative 
Commissioners as well as orders denying registration under Section 12A or under 
Section 80G of the Income -tax Act 1961.  It functions as the final fact finding 
authority in the matters c oncerning Income -tax, wealth -tax, gift -tax etc. The orders 
passed by the ITAT are final; an appeal lies to the High Court only if a substantial 
question of law arises for determination. The Tribunal consists of 63 Benches, which 
is spread over 30 stations (including 02 Circuit Benches) throughout the country.  
(iii) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body 
constituted under Section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and it has been empowered, 
among other things, to lay down standards for professional conduct and etiquette for 
lawyers, and to maintain and improve standards of legal education in the country.  
(iv) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute is a premier legal research 
institute founded on 27th December, 1956. The prime objective of the Institute is to 
promote advanced studies and research in law and to contribute substantially in 
reforming the administration of justice, so as to meet the socio-economic aspirations 
of the people through law and its instrumentalities. The Institute has been granted 
Deemed University status in the year 2004. 
(v) The India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC):- The IIAC has been 
established with a view to provide cost effective and timely services for the conduct 
of arbitration and conciliation at national and international level, facilitate conduct of 
international and domestic arbitration and conciliation and impart training in 
alternative dispute resolution and related matters in field of arbitration, conciliation 
and mediation. Its purpose is to bring reforms in the field of arbitration and 
conciliation and to develop it as a flagship institution for domestic and international 
arbitration. It will facilitate and provide administrative assistance for conduct of 
arbitration and conciliation proceedings in a professional and time-bound manner and 
in the most cost-effective way. It will also set up an arbitration chamber to empanel 
professional arbitrators at national and international level and set up an Arbitration 

 13 
Academy to train arbitrators in India, so as to empower them to compete on par with 
reputed arbitral institutions in the world. With the coming into force of the New Delhi 
International Arbitration Centre (Amendment) Act, 2022 the Centre has been renamed 
as India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC).  The Centre was notified on 26th 
July 2019. Justice Hemant Gupta, retired Judge, Supreme Court of India was 
appointed as Chairperson, of the Centre vide notification dated 23.12.2022.  Shri 
Ganesh Chandru and Shri Anant Vijay Palli have been appointed as Part-time 
Members in the Centre vide notification dated 23.12.2022. The Central Government 
has nominated Director General, Federation of Indian Export Organizations as Part-
time Member of the Centre and the Financial Adviser, Ministry of Law & Justice as 
ex-officio Member. Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs is also the ex-officio 
Member of the Centre.

2.13 The ILI in their written submissions before the Committee has informed that the 
Institute is presently facing the following functional difficulties due to shortage of funds:  
 Since the expenses are persistently rising and funds are very limited, the Institute 
is not in a position to expand its activities due to shortage of funds. 
 The Institute is not in a position to renovate Class Rooms, Halls and other 
infrastructural developments due to paucity of funds.  
 All computers, servers and other IT related infrastructure of the Institute are 
mostly outdated and funds are needed for replacement of systems with latest 
configuration to avoid cyber security threats. 
 The Institute also needs funds to enhance research publications, books and other 
legal research activities. 
 It is also pertinent to mention that the Institute is facing huge difficulties in 
filling-up all vacant positions due to deficiency of funds. 
2.14 The ILI has further informed that research is one of the major focal point of ILI and 
its faculties are encouraged to take up research activities in interdisciplinary and 
contemporary issues. ILI provides full support in terms of administrative, academic and 
infrastructure facilities to enable faculty to take up projects. The academic findings of 
research work carried out by the Institute have been beneficial for the society at large. 
Faculty are engaged in active research by way of publication of books and articles in national 

 19 
& international journals. The proceedings of National and International Conferences/ 
Seminars are routine work of ILI, which educate the students as well as Faculty. Various 
Ministries have been allocating projects to the Institute on contemporary issues and findings 
of those studies are taken note of by the Government.  
2.15 From the submission of the Institute and analysis of the functioning of the ILI 
over the years, the Committee is constrained to observe that a premier institution 
founded for promoting and conducting legal research is becoming insignificant day-by-
day due to lack of funding from the Government. Faculty positions are remaining 
vacant, basic renovation and upkeep of the institution are held up due to lack of funds. 
Only a skeletal faculty/staff are maintained with the limited grants provided by the 
Government. As we don't have many institutions in the country for legal research and 
thus, the Government should maintain this institution and not let it die a slow death. 
The Committee wants to see the Institute to become a centre of excellence in the field of 
legal research, for which it requires the support of the Government. However, the 
Committee feels that if the Government is not in a position to maintain this institute, it 
is better to hand it over to some other institutions like Supreme Court of India or BCI 
etc., like they did in case of Institute of Constitutional & Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) 
which was handed over to the Lok Sabha Secretariat.

Arbitration Centre (IIAC) (erstwhile New Delhi International Arbitration Centre) 13th June,

of the Centre. The Department has informed that the Centre is presently at an advanced stage 
of the process of framing of the Regulations inter alia for empanelment of arbitrators and the 
conduct of arbitration. Simultaneously, the Centre is in the process of augmenting its 
physical and Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure to provide for 
world class facilities to the parties, for the conduct of arbitration.  
2.17 Since the Centre was not functional prior to the appointment of the Chairperson and 
all Members, the funds granted to the Centre in the past years could not be utilized. However, 
now with the Centre having become functional with the aforesaid appointments and having 
immediate requirements of augmenting its physical and ICT infrastructure along with other 
operational necessities. For the said purpose the Centre has proposed a budgetary demand of 
Rs. 9 crores for the financial year 2023-2024. However, in B.E. 2023-24, only a total amount 
of Rs. 3 crores has been allocated, which is insufficient, for the purpose. 
2.18 The IIAC has been established with a view to compete with other reputed 
international arbitration centers and to strengthen an independent & autonomous 
arbitration regime in the Country. Though the Centre has now been formally created, 
but is still in its infancy, the Committee recommends the Government to provide it full 
financial support for creating the necessary infrastructure it needs for making it fully 
operational.

BAR COUNCIL OF INDIA (BCI) 
 
3.36 The Bar Council of India (BCI) is a statutory body constituted under the Advocates 
Act, 1961, which has been empowered among other things to lay down standards of 
professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers, maintain and improve the standard of legal 
education in the country and enforce discipline among the lawyers. The BCI also acts as an 
appellate authority in respect of disciplinary matters.  
3.37  The Bar Council of India (BCI) in its written submission before the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants (2022-23) had informed the Committee that lawyers in the country 
neither have any social security nor any protection from either State of Union Government. 
There is also lack of proper infrastructure and other facilities like sitting space, clean 
drinking water, electricity, libraries, medical aid, health insurance etc. for advocates in 
various courts.  
3.38 The BCI had further submitted that due to lack of funds, Bar Associations are not in a 
position to purchase law journals, computers, wifi facilities an d so forth, which hinders 
practice of law. The BCI has also highlighted the plight of advocates due to Covid -19 and 
has submitted that many advocates have died and dependents of advocates are facing acute 
financial problems affecting their livelihood. The BCI accordingly requested this Committee 
to consider recommending grants for the purpose through Bar Councils/Associations in order 
to carry out the welfare activities and also to meet the medical aid, health insurance facilities, 
and also library/other infrastructure facilities of Bar Associations. 
3.39 Accordingly, the Committee in its 115 th Report, which was presented to the 
Parliament on 24 th March, 2022 had recommended the Government to grant BCI the 
requisite funds for lawyers welfare including improvement of infrastructure for Bar, 
medical aid, health insurance etc. The Department had also assured the Committee that 
they will consider any s uch grant of funds for lawyers' welfare, if any such proposal is 
received from the BCI. 
3.40 However, even after elapse of about a year, the Department has not received any 
such proposal on grants for lawyers' welfare from the BCI's side. Further, the BCI has 
not furnished their comments/action taken report on the said report of the Committee 
which was required to be furnished within 3 months. Subsequently, they were again 
asked by the Committee in 125 th Report to submit their comments, but till date nothin g 
has been heard from the BCI's side.   
3.41 Further, d uring the examination of Demands for Grants for the year 2023 -24, 
the BCI has not furnished any document or reply to the questionnaire sent by the 
Committee. They even didn't attend the meeting held in  this regard on 17 th February, 
2023 citing their preoccupation with the court work.  

 34 
3.42 From the above, it may be inferred that the BCI is not serious enough in 
securing grants from the Government for lawyers' welfare. Further, non -furnishing of 
replies and action taken reports to Committee's recommendations can be seen as 
running away from parliamentary scrutiny. 
3.43 Lawyers' Welfare is an important issue and the Committee is deeply concerned 
about the welfare needs of the lawyers of the Country. The pa ndemic has underlined 
the need for having a robust welfare scheme for the lawyers to provide necessary 
assistance to lawyers and their families during the time of their need and during 
calamities. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department to exp lore the 
ways and means by which such schemes can be initiated from their side. As the 
Department is also administering the Advocates' Welfare Fund Act, 2001, they may 
also suggest if any scheme or assistance may be rolled out under this Act.

ITAT 
1. Out of the 30 Benches from which the ITAT is operating, only on 3 locations 
they are having their own building. On other 20 locations they are operating

bodies and on 7 locations from buildings of private owners. Thus there is an 
urgent need to augment and enhance the infrastructural needs of the Tribunal.

funds to ITAT to complete their ongoing projects on schedule. The Department 
should approach the MoF to get the funds required for the FY 2023-24 so that 
the ongoing projects are not stalled due to scanty allocations. (2.11) 
ILI 
2. From the submission of the Institute and analysis of the functioning of the ILI 
over the years, the Committee is constrained to observe that a premier 
institution founded for promoting and conducting legal research is becoming 
insignificant day-by-day due to lack of funding from the Government. Faculty 
positions are remaining vacant, basic renovation and upkeep of the institution 
are held up due to lack of funds. Only a skeletal faculty/staff are maintained 
with the limited grants provided by the Government. As we don't have many 
institutions in the country for legal research and thus, the Government should 
maintain this institution and not let it die a slow death. The Committee wants to 
see the Institute to become a centre of excellence in the field of legal research, for 
which it requires the support of the Government. However, the Committee feels 
that if the Government is not in a position to maintain this institute, it is better to 
hand it over to some other institutions like Supreme Court of India or BCI etc., 
like they did in case of Institute of Constitutional & Parliamentary Studies 
(ICPS) which was handed over to the Lok Sabha Secretariat. (2.15)
